**Surat al-Mutaffifin (The Defrauders)**
Thirty-six verses, Meccan

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿Woe to the defrauders,﴾ ﴿who, when they take a measure from people, take it in full,﴾ ﴿but when they measure or weigh for them, they give less.﴾

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿Woe to the defrauders,﴾ ﴿who, when they take a measure from people, take it in full,﴾ ﴿but when they measure or weigh for them, they give less.﴾

Know that the connection between the beginning of this surah and the end of the preceding surah is evident, because in the closing part of that surah God explained that the Day of Resurrection is a day in which no soul will have power to do anything for another soul, and the command on that day belongs entirely to God. This implies a great threat to the disobedient, so He followed it with His words: ﴿Woe to the defrauders.﴾ The purpose is to deter from *tatfif* (defrauding), which is cheating in measure and weight by taking a small amount secretly. The reason is that a large amount would be noticed and prevented, and even a small amount, if it became apparent, would also be prevented. Thus we know that *tatfif* is cheating in measure and weight by a small amount in secret. Here there are several issues.

The first issue: *Woe* (*al-Waylu*) is a word used when calamity befalls, as in the expressions "Woe to you" and "Woe upon you."

The second issue: concerning the derivation of the word *mutaffif* (defrauder), there are two opinions. The first is that *tuff* (طَفّ) of a thing is its side or edge. It is said: "The valley's edge (*tuff al-wadi*) and the vessel's edge," when the contents reach the rim of the vessel but it is not full. Hence it is said: *tifaf* and *tafaf* and *tafaf* (the level near the brim), and it is said: "This is the *tuff* of the measure and its *tafaf*," when it nearly reaches full but is not yet full. For this reason, the one who measures badly and does not fill it is called *mutaffif*, meaning that he only reaches the near-brim.

The second opinion, which is the view of al-Zajjaj: the one who diminishes the measure and the scale is called *mutaffif* because he is the one who steals from the measure and the scale only a small, slight amount. Here there are questions:

The first question: *iktiyal* (taking by measure) means taking by measure, just as *ittizan* means taking by weight. Furthermore, the usual idiom is to say *iktaltu min fulan* (I took by measure from so-and-so), not *iktaltu ʿala fulan* (I took by measure upon so-and-so). What is the reason for it here?

The answer: there are two aspects. The first: since their taking from people by measure was a taking that involved harm to them and oppression against them, the preposition *ʿala* (upon) was used in place of the one that indicates this. The second: al-Farra' said: the intended meaning is "they took from people," and *ʿala* and *min* in this place are interchangeable, because it is a right owed by him. So when one says "I took by measure upon you," it is as if he said "I took what is due upon you," and when one says "I took by measure from you," it is like his saying "I took my full due from you."

The second question: the usual idiom is to say *kalu lahum* (they measured for them) or *wazanu lahum* (they weighed for them), not *kiltuhu* or *wazantuhu*. So what is the reason for God's words: ﴿but when they measure or weigh for them﴾?

The answer comes in several aspects. The first: the intended meaning of His words ﴿measure or weigh for them﴾ is *kalu lahum* or *wazanu lahum*, so the preposition is omitted and the verb is made to reach the object directly. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: this is from the speech of the people of the Hijaz, and those who live near them say: *zini kadha* (weigh this), *kili kadha* (measure this), and they say *siduka* and *sidtu laka* (I hunted for you), and *kasabtuka* and *kasabtu laka* (I earned for you). According to this, the pronoun in *kalu-hum* and *wazanu-hum* is in the accusative position.

The second: it may be by omitting a noun modified and placing the noun it modifies in its place, the implied meaning being: "when they measured their measured goods, or weighed their weighed goods."

The third: it is narrated from Isa ibn Umar and Hamza that they would make the two pronouns an emphasis for what is in *kalu* (the verb), and they would pause at the two waws (in *kalu-hum* and *wazanu-hum*) with a brief pause by which they would make clear what they intended. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj claimed this is not permissible, because if it meant *kalu-hum*, there would be a written alif in the *Mushaf* before *hum*. Sahib al-Kashshaf objected to this argument and said that the orthography of the *Mushaf* did not observe, in much of it, the rules established in the science of orthography.

The answer to this: if the writing of this alif had not been customary in the time of the Companions, it would have been necessary for it to be written in all later periods, since we know their great care in this matter. So it is established that writing this alif was customary in the time of the Companions, and therefore it would have been necessary to write it here.

The third question: what is the reason that He said ﴿Woe to the defrauders, who, when they take by measure﴾ and did not say *idha ittazanu* (when they take by weight), then said ﴿but when they measure or weigh for them﴾ and so combined the two? The answer: measuring and weighing are the means of buying and selling, so one of them indicates the other.

The fourth question: the usual idiom is to say *kharistuhu* (I caused him loss), so what is the reason for *akhsartuhu* (I caused him to lose)?

The answer: al-Zajjaj said: *akhsartu al-mizan* and *kharistuhu* are the same, meaning I diminished it. And from al-Mu'arrij: *yukhsiruna* means *yanqusuna* (they diminish), in the dialect of Quraysh.

The third issue: on the authority of ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: When the Prophet of God arrived in Medina, they were among the most dishonest of people in measuring. So God revealed this verse, and after that they measured well. It was also said: the people of Medina were merchants who defrauded, and their trading was by *munabadha* (throwing a garment as a sale without inspection), *mulamasa* (touching as a sale), and *mukhatara* (gambling-type sales). So this verse was revealed, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out and recited it to them and said: "Five for five." It was asked: "O Messenger of God, what is 'five for five'?" He said: "No people break a covenant except that God gives their enemy power over them; no people judge by other than what God has revealed except that poverty spreads among them; no indecency appears among a people except that death spreads among them; they do not defraud in measure except that they are denied vegetation and seized by years of drought; and they do not withhold zakat except that rain is withheld from them."

The fourth issue: the blame falls upon them only for the combination of their taking more and giving less. Then the scholars differed. Some said: this verse indicates a threat, so it does not apply unless the defrauding reaches the level of a large amount, which is the threshold for theft. Others said: rather, whether small or large, it falls under the threat, but on the condition that there is no repentance or obedience greater than it with it. This is the more correct view.

The fifth issue: the people of *al-wa'id* (the threat, i.e., the Mu'tazilah) argued from the generality of this verse. They said: this verse is addressed to people of prayer, not to disbelievers. What indicates this are two aspects.

The first: if he were a disbeliever, that disbelief would be more deserving of this woe than defrauding, so defrauding would have no effect on this woe; but the verse indicates that what necessitates this woe is defrauding.

The second: God said to those addressed in this verse: ﴿Do they not think that they will be resurrected, for a tremendous Day?﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 4–5]. So it is as if He threatened the defrauders with the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, and such a threat is applicable only to a believer. Thus it is established by these two aspects that this threat is specific to the people of prayer.

The answer to this is what has been stated many times before. Among the corollaries of this issue is that this threat encompasses both one who does this and one who intends to do it, since intending it is also among the major sins.

Know that the matter of measure and weight is great, because most of creation needs transactions, and transactions are based on measure and weight. For this reason God magnified its matter, saying: ﴿And the sky He raised, and He set the balance﴾ [al-Rahman: 7], ﴿that you not transgress in the balance﴾ [al-Rahman: 8], ﴿and establish weight with justice and do not diminish the balance﴾ [al-Rahman: 9]. And He said: ﴿We sent Our messengers with clear proofs and sent down with them the Scripture and the balance, that people may uphold justice﴾ [al-Hadid: 25].

It is narrated from Qatadah: "Give full measure, O son of Adam, as you love to be given full measure, and be just as you love to be treated justly." And from al-Fudayl: "The diminishing of the balance is blackness of the face on the Day of Resurrection."

A Bedouin said to ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwan: "You have heard what God said about the defrauders!" He meant by this that the defrauder has been subjected to a great threat for taking a small amount, so what is your opinion of yourself, when you take a large amount and take the wealth of the Muslims without measure or weight?

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 83, verses 4–6:**

Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Do they not think that they will be resurrected﴾ ﴿for a tremendous Day﴾ ﴿the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾.

Know that Allah, exalted is He, rebuked these defrauders (al-Mutaffifin) and said: ﴿Do they not think﴾ (those who defraud) ﴿that they will be resurrected for a tremendous Day﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection. Regarding the word "ẓann" (thinking/supposing) here, there are two opinions.

The first: it is meant to signify knowledge (ʿilm). On this reading, the people addressed by this address may be among those who affirm the resurrection, or they may not be. As for the first possibility: it is narrated that the Muslims of Madinah, namely the Aws and the Khazraj, were like this, and when the Prophet (ﷺ) arrived, this was widespread among them, and they affirmed the resurrection and rising again. Therefore they were reminded of it. As for if we say that those addressed by this verse did not believe in the resurrection, but they were capable of reasoning about it, due to what is in the intellects regarding the delivery of recompense to the good-doer and the evil-doer, or the possibility of that if its obligation is not established, then this is something that may be addressed to one who denies the resurrection. The meaning is: "Will they not reflect until they know that they will be resurrected?" But they have turned away from reflection and relieved themselves of its burdens and hardships. Reasoning is called "ẓann" only because most rational sciences rest on what is most probable in opinion, and it is not like doubt, in which the two sides are equal. Therefore it was called ẓann.

The second opinion: the word ẓann here means actual supposition and not knowledge. The meaning is: even if these defrauders do not affirm the resurrection with certainty, at least they should suppose it. For the wisdom, mercy and care of Allah for the interests of His creation fit better with not leaving their affair entirely neglected after death, and that there should be for them a gathering and a raising. This supposition is sufficient to produce fear. It is as if He, glorified and exalted, is saying: "Even if these people do not hold it with certainty, will they not at least suppose it?" As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: the word "yawm" (Day) has been read in the accusative and in the genitive. As for the accusative, al-Zajjaj said: "yawm" is in the accusative, governed by the word "mabʿūthūn" (will be resurrected), and the meaning is: "Do they not suppose that they will be raised on the Day of Resurrection?" Al-Farra' said: "It may also be in the genitive position, but it has been made an annexed noun to the verb (yaf'ulu) and so it is in the accusative, and this is like what we mentioned regarding His saying: ﴿the Day when no soul will have power for another﴾." As for the genitive, it is because it is in apposition (badal) to "a tremendous Day."

The second issue: this standing has attributes.

The first attribute: its cause, and concerning it there are several aspects.

One of them, which is the most correct, is that people stand for the reckoning before the Lord of the worlds, and there this defrauding will appear, which was thought to be trivial, and there its magnitude and its accumulation will be known. Close to this is His saying: ﴿And for the one who fears the standing before his Lord there are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 46].

The second: He, glorified is He, returns the spirits to their bodies, and those bodies rise from their resting places. That is what is meant by His saying: ﴿the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾.

The third: Abu Muslim said that the meaning of "yaqūm al-nās" (mankind stands) is like His saying: ﴿And stand before Allah in devotion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238], that is, for His worship. So His saying ﴿mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾ means purely for His command and obedience, and not for anything else, as he established in His saying: ﴿And the command on that Day belongs to Allah﴾ [al-Infitar: 19].

The second attribute: the manner of that standing. It was narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying ﴿the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾, that he said: "One of you will stand in his sweat up to the middle of his ears." And from Ibn ʿUmar: that he recited this surah, and when he reached His saying ﴿the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾ he wept intensely until he was unable to recite what came after it.

The third attribute: the duration of that standing. It was narrated from him (peace be upon him) that he said: "People will stand for the length of three hundred years of the world, with no command given concerning them." And from Ibn Masʿud: "They will remain forty years, then they will be addressed." Ibn ʿAbbas said: for the believers it is like the duration of their leaving from the prayer.

Know that Allah, glorified is He, has gathered in this verse several kinds of threat. He first said: ﴿Woe to the defrauders﴾, and this word is mentioned at the descent of calamity. Then He said second: ﴿Do they not think that they will be resurrected﴾, which is a question carrying the meaning of denunciation. Then He said third: ﴿for a tremendous Day﴾, and the thing that Allah considers tremendous is undoubtedly at the utmost of greatness. Then He said fourth: ﴿the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾, and in this there are two kinds of threat.

One of them: that they will be standing with the utmost humility, the extreme of abasement and submission.

The second: that He described Himself as being the Lord of the worlds.

Then here there is a question, as if someone said: How is it fitting for You, with Your utmost greatness, to prepare this mighty assembly, which is the assembly of the Resurrection, for the sake of a lowly and trivial matter? So He, glorified is He, responds, saying: The majesty of divinity is not complete except with greatness in power and greatness in wisdom. The greatness of power has appeared through My being Lord of the worlds. But the greatness of wisdom does not appear except by My granting justice to the oppressed against the oppressor, on account of that lowly and trivial amount. For whenever a thing is more base and smaller, the knowledge that reaches it is greater and more complete. Therefore, for the sake of displaying greatness in wisdom, I have brought together the creation of the first and the last at the assembly of the Resurrection, and I have called the defrauder to account for that trivial amount.

Al-Ustadh Abu al-Qasim al-Qushayri said: The word "mutaffif" (defrauder) encompasses defrauding in weighing and measuring, and in revealing faults and concealing them, and in seeking fairness and seeking to have justice done. It is said: whoever does not wish for his Muslim brother what he wishes for himself is not fair. Companionship and fellowship fall under this category. Whoever looks at the faults of people but does not look at his own fault is of this category. Whoever seeks his own rights from people but does not give them their rights as he seeks his own is of this category. The noble youth is one who fulfills the rights of people and does not ask anyone for a right for himself.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 83, verses 7–17 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Nay! Indeed the record of the wicked is in Sijjin.﴾ ﴿And what will make you know what Sijjin is?﴾ ﴿It is a written record.﴾ ﴿Woe on that day to the deniers,﴾ ﴿who deny the Day of Judgment.﴾ ﴿None deny it except every transgressor, sinful,﴾ ﴿when Our verses are recited to him he says, "Tales of the ancients."﴾ ﴿Nay! Rather, what they used to earn has covered over their hearts.﴾ ﴿Nay! Indeed they, that day, will be veiled from their Lord.﴾ ﴿Then indeed they will be burning in Hellfire.﴾ ﴿Then it will be said, "This is what you used to deny."﴾

Know that when He, glorified is He, explained the magnitude of this sin, He followed it with mention of its consequences and rulings. The first of these is His saying "Nay" (kallā). The exegetes have mentioned several views concerning it.

The first: it is a rebuke and an admonition, meaning the matter is not as they are, in their short-measure and heedlessness regarding the mention of resurrection and reckoning, so let them desist. The complete statement ends here.

The second: Abu Hatim said: "Kallā" is a beginning that connects with what follows, in the sense of "truly, ﴿indeed the record of the wicked is in Sijjin﴾." This is also the view of al-Hasan.

The second type: He, the Exalted, described the record of the wicked with baseness and worthlessness, by way of belittling them. Here there are questions.

The first question: Is Sijjin a proper noun for a specific thing, or a derived noun from a meaning? We say there are two opinions:

The first, which is the view of the majority of exegetes: it is a proper noun for a specific thing. Then they differed about it. Most hold that it is the seventh, lowest earth. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas in the narration of ʿAta', and of Qatada, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd. Al-Bara' narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "Sijjin is the lowest of the seven earths." ʿAta' al-Khurasani said: in it are Iblis and his offspring. Abu Hurayra narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "Sijjin is a pit in Hell." Al-Kalbi and Mujahid said: Sijjin is a rock beneath the seventh earth.

The second opinion: it is derived, named Sijjin as a form of fi‘dl from the prison (sijn), which is confinement and constriction, as one says fisiq from fisq. This is the view of Abu ʿUbayda, al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj. Al-Wahidi said: this is weak, and the evidence that Sijjin is not something the Arabs knew is His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what Sijjin is?﴾, meaning that this is not something you and your people knew. I say: it is not weak, for perhaps He mentioned it only to magnify the matter of Sijjin, as in His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Judgment is?﴾ The author of "al-Kashshaf" said: the correct view is that Sijjin is a fi‘īl form derived from the prison (sijn); then here it is a proper name transferred from an adjective, like Hatim, and it is diptote, because it has only one cause, which is definiteness.

Having known this, we say: We have mentioned that Allah, the Exalted, dealt with His servants in matters according to what they are accustomed to in their dealings among themselves and with their great ones. So Paradise is described with height, purity, spaciousness and the presence of the nearest angels, while Sijjin is described with lowliness, darkness, constriction and the presence of the accursed devils. There is no doubt that height, purity, spaciousness and the presence of the nearest angels are all attributes of perfection and honor, and their opposites are attributes of deficiency and abasement. So when the description of the disbelievers and their record in abasement and worthlessness was intended, it was said that it is in the place of lowliness, darkness, constriction and the presence of devils. And when He described the record of the righteous with honor, it was said that it is ﴿in ʿIlliyyun﴾ and ﴿witnessed by those brought near﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 17].

The second question: Allah has informed about the record of the wicked that it is ﴿in Sijjin﴾, then He explained Sijjin with ﴿a written record﴾. So it is as if it were said: their record is in a written record, so what is its meaning? Al-Qaffal answered: his saying ﴿a written record﴾ is not an explanation of Sijjin; rather the construction is: "Nay! Indeed the record of the wicked is in Sijjin, and indeed the record of the wicked is a written record," so this is a description of the record of the wicked with two attributes: one, that it is in Sijjin; and two, that it is written. And ﴿And what will make you know what Sijjin is?﴾ falls between the two descriptions as a parenthetical interjection. And Allah knows best.

It is better to say: what is strange about one of the two records being within the other? Either the record of the wicked is placed in the book that is the source referred to for detailing the states of the wretched, or what is in the record of the wicked is transferred to that book named Sijjin. There is also a third view: that the intended meaning of "kitāb" is writing, so the sense is: the writing of the wicked is in Sijjin, meaning the writing of their deeds is in Sijjin; then Sijjin is described as ﴿a written record﴾ containing all the deeds of the wicked.

The third question: What is the meaning of His saying ﴿a written record﴾? We say there are several views:

One: "marqūm" means their deeds are written in it.

Second: Qatada said: it was marked for them with evil, meaning it was written for them with the necessity of the Fire.

Third: al-Qaffal said: it may be that what is meant is that He made that record marked, as a merchant marks his garment with a sign of its price; so likewise the record of the wicked is made marked with a mark indicating his wretchedness.

Fourth: "al-marqūm" here means "al-makhtūm" (sealed). Al-Wahidi said: this is correct, because sealing is a sign, so it is permissible to call the marked "sealed."

Fifth: the meaning is a record established upon them like the marking on a garment that does not fade.

As for His saying ﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾, there are two views concerning it:

One: it is connected to His saying ﴿the day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds﴾, meaning: ﴿the day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds﴾, woe to whoever denied the reports of Allah.

Two: His saying "marqūm" means it was marked with a mark indicating wretchedness on the Day of Resurrection; then He said ﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾, on that day, from that record. Then He informed about the description of those who deny the Day of Judgment, saying: ﴿None deny it except every transgressor, sinful, when Our verses are recited to him he says, "Tales of the ancients."﴾ And its meaning is that none denies the Day of Judgment except one who has these three attributes.

The first of them: being a transgressor, and transgression is going beyond the true path.

The second: the sinful, which is an intensive form of committing sin and disobedience. I say: man has two faculties: a theoretical faculty whose perfection lies in knowing the truth for its own sake, and a practical faculty whose perfection lies in knowing the good for the sake of acting upon it. The opposite of the first is to describe Allah with what is not permissible to attribute to Him, for everyone who denies the possibility of resurrection and the Last Day denies either because he did not know that Allah's knowledge encompasses all knowables, universal and particular, or because he did not know that Allah's power extends to all possibilities. So this transgression is the opposite of the practical faculty, namely being occupied with desire and anger, and its possessor is the sinful, because one occupied with desire and anger rarely finds leisure for worship and obedience, and this may well become an obstacle for him to faith in the Last Day.

As for the third attribute of those who deny the Day of Judgment, it is His saying ﴿when Our verses are recited to him he says, "Tales of the ancients."﴾ What is meant are those who deny prophethood. The meaning is: when the Qur'an is recited to him, he says, "Tales of the ancients." And there are two views: one, the falsehoods of the ancients; two, the reports of the ancients, and that it was taken from them, meaning he impugns the Qur'an being from Allah by this route.

Here is another discussion: whether these three attributes refer to a specific person or not. There are two views.

The first, which is the view of al-Kalbi, is that what is meant is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. Others said it is al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. Those who held that it is al-Walid argued that He said in Surat Nun: ﴿And do not obey every oft-swearing despicable one﴾ up to His saying ﴿transgressor, sinful﴾ up to His saying ﴿when Our verses are recited to him he says, "Tales of the ancients."﴾ [al-Qalam: 10–15], so it was said that this refers to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. On this assumption the meaning is: none of the Quraysh, or of your people, denies the Day of Judgment except every transgressor, sinful; and this is the specific person.

The second view: it is general concerning all who are described with these attributes. As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Nay! Rather, what they used to earn has covered over their hearts﴾, the meaning is: the matter is not as he claims, that these are the tales of the ancients; rather their past deeds became a cause for the rust (rayn) to settle upon their hearts. The lexicographers and the exegetes have several explanations of the word rayn. As for the lexicographers, Abu ʿUbayda said: "rāna ʿalā qulūbihim" means it overcame them, and wine "yarīnu ʿalā" the intellect of the drunkard, and death "yarīnu ʿalā" the dead person so that it takes him away. Al-Layth said: sleep and wine "rāna" in the head when it takes firm hold of it, and it "yarinu" rayvan and ruyūnan. From this is the hadith of ʿUmar concerning Usayfiʿ of Juhayna, when debt overwhelmed him: "He has become overwhelmed by it (qad rīna bihi)." Abu Zayd said: one says "rīna bi-l-rajul yurānu bihi raynan" when he falls into what he cannot get out of. Abu Muʿadh al-Nahwi said: rayn is that the heart becomes blackened by sins, and ṭabʿ is that it is sealed upon the heart, which is stronger than rayn, and iqfāl is stronger than ṭabʿ, being that it is locked upon the heart. Al-Zajjaj said: "rāna ʿalā qulūbihim" means "ghashiya ʿalā qulūbihim" (covered over their hearts); one says "rāna ʿalā qalbihi al-dhanbu yarīnu raynan," i.e. sin enveloped it; and rayn is like rust covering the heart, and likewise ʿayn. As for the exegetes, they have several views: al-Hasan and Mujahid said: it is sin upon sin, until sins encompass the heart and cover it so that the heart dies. It is narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Beware of the trivial sins, for sin upon sin kindles a huge blaze upon its doer." And from Mujahid: the heart is like the palm; when one commits a sin it contracts, and when he commits another sin it contracts again, then it is sealed upon, and this is rayn. Others said: whenever a person sins, a black spot appears in his heart until the whole heart blackens. This is narrated as a marfu' hadith from Abu Hurayra. I say: there is no doubt that the repetition of acts is a cause for the acquisition of an inner disposition, for whoever wishes to learn writing, the more he practices writing the more perfect his capacity for it becomes, until he reaches the point where he can write without deliberation or thought. This inner disposition, since it was generated from those many acts, each one of those acts has an effect in producing that inner disposition. Having known this, we say: when a person persists in committing some kinds of sin, an inner disposition to commit that sin takes root in his heart, and there is no meaning to sin except what occupies you with other than Allah, and whatever occupies you with other than Allah is darkness; so all sins are darkness and blackness. And each of the past deeds, whose collective result produced that disposition, has an effect in its production. That is what is meant by their saying: whenever a person sins, a black spot appears in his heart until the heart blackens. And since the levels of dispositions differ in intensity and weakness, the levels of this blackness and darkness likewise differ; so some of it is rayn, some is ṭabʿ, and some is iqfāl. The judge said: rayn does not mean that their hearts have changed and an obstruction has occurred in them; rather it means that they became, state after state, bold toward committing sin, their motives to abandon repentance and to refrain grew strong, so they persisted and the matter became difficult for them. That is why He explained that the cause of the rayn is their earning, and it is known that their great acquisition of sins does not prevent them from ceasing and repenting. I say: we have already shown that the occurrence of an act when the motive is equal

to the act, and the motive to abandon it is impossible, because it is impossible for a possible thing to be preponderated without a preponderant cause. So, if it is impossible in the state of being outweighed, it is all the more so. And since al-Qadi conceded that they became, by means of the past deeds, preponderant, it must be that abandoning [sin] in this state is impossible. The full discussion has been presented repeatedly in this book.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay! Indeed, they will be veiled from their Lord that Day﴾, know that they have mentioned several interpretations of (kallā, "nay").

The first: The author of al-Kashshaf said: (kallā) is a deterrent from the gain that has covered over their hearts.

The second: al-Qaffal said: God, exalted is He, related in various surahs about this transgressing sinner that he used to say, "If the Hereafter is true, then God will surely give me wealth and children." Then God, exalted is He, refuted this claim, saying: ﴿Has he looked into the unseen, or has he taken a covenant with the Most Merciful?﴾ [Maryam: 78], and He said: ﴿I do not think the Hour will ever come; and even if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely have a better (reward) with Him﴾ [Fussilat: 50]. Since this has been mentioned repeatedly in the Qur'an, God omitted its mention here and said: ﴿Nay! Indeed, they will be veiled from their Lord that Day﴾, meaning: the matter is not as they claim, that they will have a good reward in the Hereafter; rather, they will be veiled from their Lord that Day.

Third: That this is a repetition, and that this (kallā) is the one mentioned in His saying: ﴿Nay! Rather, what they have earned has rusted over their hearts﴾. As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, they will be veiled from their Lord that Day﴾, the companions (of al-Ash'ari) have argued from it that the believers will see Him, glory be to Him. They said: Were it not so, the specification would have no purpose.

There is another argument, namely that He mentioned this veiling in the context of a threat and warning to the disbelievers, and what is a warning and threat for the disbelievers cannot apply to the believer; therefore this veiling must not apply to the believer. The Mu'tazilah answered this in several ways:

The first: al-Jubba'i said: The intended meaning is that they are veiled from the mercy of their Lord, i.e., prevented, just as it is said in the rules of inheritance: the brothers exclude the mother to a third (yahjubūna al-umm 'ala al-thuluth), and from this it is said of one who prevents entry that he is a ḥājib, because he prevents one from seeing [the ruler].

The second: Abu Muslim said: ﴿Indeed, they will be veiled﴾ means: not brought near. Ḥijāb means rejection, which is the opposite of acceptance, and the meaning is that these deniers of the Resurrection will not be accepted by God. This is what is meant by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor will God speak to them, nor look at them on the Day of Resurrection, nor purify them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 77].

The third: al-Qadi said: Ḥijāb is not an expression for the absence of seeing, for it is said: So-and-so was veiled from the amir, even though he had seen him from a distance. And if ḥijāb is not an expression for the absence of seeing, the argument falls; rather, it must be understood as becoming prevented from finding His mercy, exalted is He.

The fourth: The author of al-Kashshaf said: Their being veiled from Him is an image of contempt for them and humiliation, because access to kings is granted only to those honored in their presence, and only those despised by them are kept away.

The reply: There is no doubt that whoever is prevented from seeing something is said to be veiled from it; and likewise whoever is prevented from entering upon the amir is said to be veiled from him; and likewise it is said that the mother is veiled from the third because of the brothers. When we find these usages, it becomes necessary to take the word as literally applying to a common concept among these instances, to avoid homonymy in the word, and that concept is prevention. In the first case, prevention from seeing occurred; in the second, prevention from reaching nearness to Him; in the third, prevention from entitlement to the third. So the verse's meaning becomes: "Nay! Indeed, they will be prevented from their Lord that Day." Prevention is realized only with respect to what would be established for the servant in relation to God, exalted is He, and that is either knowledge or sight. It cannot be taken to mean knowledge, because that is established for the disbelievers by consensus; therefore it must be taken to mean sight. As for interpreting it as mercy, that is a departure from the apparent meaning without evidence; and likewise what the author of al-Kashshaf said is an abandonment of the apparent meaning without evidence. Then, what confirms the evidence we have mentioned is the statements of the exegetes.

Muqatil said: The meaning of the verse is that after the reckoning and the account, they will not see their Lord, while the believers will see their Lord. Al-Kalbi said: He says they are veiled from looking upon the vision of their Lord, whereas the believer is not veiled from the vision of his Lord. Mālik ibn Anas was asked about this verse and said: Since He veiled His enemies so that they did not see Him, it must be that He manifests Himself to His friends so that they see Him. From al-Shafi'i: Since He veiled a people by wrath, this indicates that another people will see Him by good pleasure.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then indeed they will be burning in Hell﴾, the meaning is: when they become veiled in the place of Resurrection, either from the sight of God according to our view, or from the mercy and honor of God according to the Mu'tazilah, then at that point they are commanded to Hell. Then, when they enter the Fire, they are rebuked for their denial of the Resurrection and the recompense, and it is said to them: ﴿This is what you used to deny﴾ in the world; and now you have witnessed it, so taste it.

Rather, what they used to earn has covered over their hearts.﴾ ﴿Nay! The second: Abu Hatim said: "Kallā" is a beginning that connects with what follows, in the sense of "truly, ﴿indeed the record of the wicked is in Sijjin﴾." This is also the view of al-Hasan.

The second type: He, the Exalted, described the record of the wicked with baseness and worthlessness, by way of belittling them. Here there are questions.

The first question: Is Sijjin a proper noun for a specific thing, or a derived noun from a meaning? We say there are two opinions:

The first, which is the view of the majority of exegetes: it is a proper noun for a specific thing. Then they differed about it. Most hold that it is the seventh, lowest earth. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas in the narration of ʿAta', and of Qatada, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd. Al-Bara' narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "Sijjin is the lowest of the seven earths." ʿAta' al-Khurasani said: in it are Iblis and his offspring. Abu Hurayra narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "Sijjin is a pit in Hell." Al-Kalbi and Mujahid said: Sijjin is a rock beneath the seventh earth.

The second opinion: it is derived, named Sijjin as a form of fi‘dl from the prison (sijn), which is confinement and constriction, as one says fisiq from fisq. This is the view of Abu ʿUbayda, al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj. Al-Wahidi said: this is weak, and the evidence that Sijjin is not something the Arabs knew is His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what Sijjin is?﴾, meaning that this is not something you and your people knew. I say: it is not weak, for perhaps He mentioned it only to magnify the matter of Sijjin, as in His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Judgment is?﴾ The author of "al-Kashshaf" said: the correct view is that Sijjin is a fi‘īl form derived from the prison (sijn); then here it is a proper name transferred from an adjective, like Hatim, and it is diptote, because it has only one cause, which is definiteness.

Having known this, we say: We have mentioned that Allah, the Exalted, dealt with His servants in matters according to what they are accustomed to in their dealings among themselves and with their great ones. So Paradise is described with height, purity, spaciousness and the presence of the nearest angels, while Sijjin is described with lowliness, darkness, constriction and the presence of the accursed devils. There is no doubt that height, purity, spaciousness and the presence of the nearest angels are all attributes of perfection and honor, and their opposites are attributes of deficiency and abasement. So when the description of the disbelievers and their record in abasement and worthlessness was intended, it was said that it is in the place of lowliness, darkness, constriction and the presence of devils. The second question: Allah has informed about the record of the wicked that it is ﴿in Sijjin﴾, then He explained Sijjin with ﴿a written record﴾. So it is as if it were said: their record is in a written record, so what is its meaning? Al-Qaffal answered: his saying ﴿a written record﴾ is not an explanation of Sijjin; rather the construction is: "Nay! Indeed the record of the wicked is in Sijjin, and indeed the record of the wicked is a written record," so this is a description of the record of the wicked with two attributes: one, that it is in Sijjin; and two, that it is written. And ﴿And what will make you know what Sijjin is?﴾ falls between the two descriptions as a parenthetical interjection. And Allah knows best.

It is better to say: what is strange about one of the two records being within the other? Either the record of the wicked is placed in the book that is the source referred to for detailing the states of the wretched, or what is in the record of the wicked is transferred to that book named Sijjin. There is also a third view: that the intended meaning of "kitāb" is writing, so the sense is: the writing of the wicked is in Sijjin, meaning the writing of their deeds is in Sijjin; then Sijjin is described as ﴿a written record﴾ containing all the deeds of the wicked.

The third question: What is the meaning of His saying ﴿a written record﴾? We say there are several views:

One: "marqūm" means their deeds are written in it.

Second: Qatada said: it was marked for them with evil, meaning it was written for them with the necessity of the Fire.

Third: al-Qaffal said: it may be that what is meant is that He made that record marked, as a merchant marks his garment with a sign of its price; so likewise the record of the wicked is made marked with a mark indicating his wretchedness.

Fourth: "al-marqūm" here means "al-makhtūm" (sealed). Al-Wahidi said: this is correct, because sealing is a sign, so it is permissible to call the marked "sealed."

Fifth: the meaning is a record established upon them like the marking on a garment that does not fade.

One: it is connected to His saying ﴿the day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds﴾, meaning: ﴿the day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds﴾, woe to whoever denied the reports of Allah.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 83, verses 7–17 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Nay! Indeed the record of the wicked is in Sijjin.﴾ ﴿And what will make you know what Sijjin is?﴾ ﴿It is a written record.﴾ ﴿Woe on that day to the deniers,﴾ ﴿who deny the Day of Judgment.﴾ ﴿None deny it except every transgressor, sinful,﴾ ﴿when Our verses are recited to him he says, "Tales of the ancients."﴾ ﴿Nay! Rather, what they used to earn has covered over their hearts.﴾ ﴿Nay! Indeed they, that day, will be veiled from their Lord.﴾ ﴿Then indeed they will be burning in Hellfire.﴾ ﴿Then it will be said, "This is what you used to deny."﴾

Know that when He, glorified is He, explained the magnitude of this sin, He followed it with mention of its consequences and rulings. The first of these is His saying "Nay" (kallā). The exegetes have mentioned several views concerning it.

The first: it is a rebuke and an admonition, meaning the matter is not as they are, in their short-measure and heedlessness regarding the mention of resurrection and reckoning, so let them desist. The complete statement ends here.

The second: Abu Hatim said: "Kallā" is a beginning that connects with what follows, in the sense of "truly, ﴿indeed the record of the wicked is in Sijjin﴾." This is also the view of al-Hasan.

The second type: He, the Exalted, described the record of the wicked with baseness and worthlessness, by way of belittling them. Here there are questions.

The first question: Is Sijjin a proper noun for a specific thing, or a derived noun from a meaning? We say there are two opinions:

The first, which is the view of the majority of exegetes: it is a proper noun for a specific thing. Then they differed about it. Most hold that it is the seventh, lowest earth. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas in the narration of ʿAta', and of Qatada, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd. Al-Bara' narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "Sijjin is the lowest of the seven earths." ʿAta' al-Khurasani said: in it are Iblis and his offspring. Abu Hurayra narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "Sijjin is a pit in Hell." Al-Kalbi and Mujahid said: Sijjin is a rock beneath the seventh earth.

The second opinion: it is derived, named Sijjin as a form of fi‘dl from the prison (sijn), which is confinement and constriction, as one says fisiq from fisq. This is the view of Abu ʿUbayda, al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj. Al-Wahidi said: this is weak, and the evidence that Sijjin is not something the Arabs knew is His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what Sijjin is?﴾, meaning that this is not something you and your people knew. I say: it is not weak, for perhaps He mentioned it only to magnify the matter of Sijjin, as in His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Judgment is?﴾ The author of "al-Kashshaf" said: the correct view is that Sijjin is a fi‘īl form derived from the prison (sijn); then here it is a proper name transferred from an adjective, like Hatim, and it is diptote, because it has only one cause, which is definiteness.

Having known this, we say: We have mentioned that Allah, the Exalted, dealt with His servants in matters according to what they are accustomed to in their dealings among themselves and with their great ones. So Paradise is described with height, purity, spaciousness and the presence of the nearest angels, while Sijjin is described with lowliness, darkness, constriction and the presence of the accursed devils. There is no doubt that height, purity, spaciousness and the presence of the nearest angels are all attributes of perfection and honor, and their opposites are attributes of deficiency and abasement. So when the description of the disbelievers and their record in abasement and worthlessness was intended, it was said that it is in the place of lowliness, darkness, constriction and the presence of devils. And when He described the record of the righteous with honor, it was said that it is ﴿in ʿIlliyyun﴾ and ﴿witnessed by those brought near﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 17].

The second question: Allah has informed about the record of the wicked that it is ﴿in Sijjin﴾, then He explained Sijjin with ﴿a written record﴾. So it is as if it were said: their record is in a written record, so what is its meaning? Al-Qaffal answered: his saying ﴿a written record﴾ is not an explanation of Sijjin; rather the construction is: "Nay! Indeed the record of the wicked is in Sijjin, and indeed the record of the wicked is a written record," so this is a description of the record of the wicked with two attributes: one, that it is in Sijjin; and two, that it is written. And ﴿And what will make you know what Sijjin is?﴾ falls between the two descriptions as a parenthetical interjection. And Allah knows best.

It is better to say: what is strange about one of the two records being within the other? Either the record of the wicked is placed in the book that is the source referred to for detailing the states of the wretched, or what is in the record of the wicked is transferred to that book named Sijjin. There is also a third view: that the intended meaning of "kitāb" is writing, so the sense is: the writing of the wicked is in Sijjin, meaning the writing of their deeds is in Sijjin; then Sijjin is described as ﴿a written record﴾ containing all the deeds of the wicked.

The third question: What is the meaning of His saying ﴿a written record﴾? We say there are several views:

One: "marqūm" means their deeds are written in it.

Second: Qatada said: it was marked for them with evil, meaning it was written for them with the necessity of the Fire.

Third: al-Qaffal said: it may be that what is meant is that He made that record marked, as a merchant marks his garment with a sign of its price; so likewise the record of the wicked is made marked with a mark indicating his wretchedness.

Fourth: "al-marqūm" here means "al-makhtūm" (sealed). Al-Wahidi said: this is correct, because sealing is a sign, so it is permissible to call the marked "sealed."

Fifth: the meaning is a record established upon them like the marking on a garment that does not fade.

As for His saying ﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾, there are two views concerning it:

One: it is connected to His saying ﴿the day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds﴾, meaning: ﴿the day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds﴾, woe to whoever denied the reports of Allah.

Two: His saying "marqūm" means it was marked with a mark indicating wretchedness on the Day of Resurrection; then He said ﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾, on that day, from that record. Then He informed about the description of those who deny the Day of Judgment, saying: ﴿None deny it except every transgressor, sinful, when Our verses are recited to him he says, "Tales of the ancients."﴾ And its meaning is that none denies the Day of Judgment except one who has these three attributes.

The first of them: being a transgressor, and transgression is going beyond the true path.

The second: the sinful, which is an intensive form of committing sin and disobedience. I say: man has two faculties: a theoretical faculty whose perfection lies in knowing the truth for its own sake, and a practical faculty whose perfection lies in knowing the good for the sake of acting upon it. The opposite of the first is to describe Allah with what is not permissible to attribute to Him, for everyone who denies the possibility of resurrection and the Last Day denies either because he did not know that Allah's knowledge encompasses all knowables, universal and particular, or because he did not know that Allah's power extends to all possibilities. So this transgression is the opposite of the practical faculty, namely being occupied with desire and anger, and its possessor is the sinful, because one occupied with desire and anger rarely finds leisure for worship and obedience, and this may well become an obstacle for him to faith in the Last Day.

As for the third attribute of those who deny the Day of Judgment, it is His saying ﴿when Our verses are recited to him he says, "Tales of the ancients."﴾ What is meant are those who deny prophethood. The meaning is: when the Qur'an is recited to him, he says, "Tales of the ancients." And there are two views: one, the falsehoods of the ancients; two, the reports of the ancients, and that it was taken from them, meaning he impugns the Qur'an being from Allah by this route.

Here is another discussion: whether these three attributes refer to a specific person or not. There are two views.

The first, which is the view of al-Kalbi, is that what is meant is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. Others said it is al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. Those who held that it is al-Walid argued that He said in Surat Nun: ﴿And do not obey every oft-swearing despicable one﴾ up to His saying ﴿transgressor, sinful﴾ up to His saying ﴿when Our verses are recited to him he says, "Tales of the ancients."﴾ [al-Qalam: 10–15], so it was said that this refers to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. On this assumption the meaning is: none of the Quraysh, or of your people, denies the Day of Judgment except every transgressor, sinful; and this is the specific person.

The second view: it is general concerning all who are described with these attributes. As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Nay! Rather, what they used to earn has covered over their hearts﴾, the meaning is: the matter is not as he claims, that these are the tales of the ancients; rather their past deeds became a cause for the rust (rayn) to settle upon their hearts. The lexicographers and the exegetes have several explanations of the word rayn. As for the lexicographers, Abu ʿUbayda said: "rāna ʿalā qulūbihim" means it overcame them, and wine "yarīnu ʿalā" the intellect of the drunkard, and death "yarīnu ʿalā" the dead person so that it takes him away. Al-Layth said: sleep and wine "rāna" in the head when it takes firm hold of it, and it "yarinu" rayvan and ruyūnan. From this is the hadith of ʿUmar concerning Usayfiʿ of Juhayna, when debt overwhelmed him: "He has become overwhelmed by it (qad rīna bihi)." Abu Zayd said: one says "rīna bi-l-rajul yurānu bihi raynan" when he falls into what he cannot get out of. Abu Muʿadh al-Nahwi said: rayn is that the heart becomes blackened by sins, and ṭabʿ is that it is sealed upon the heart, which is stronger than rayn, and iqfāl is stronger than ṭabʿ, being that it is locked upon the heart. Al-Zajjaj said: "rāna ʿalā qulūbihim" means "ghashiya ʿalā qulūbihim" (covered over their hearts); one says "rāna ʿalā qalbihi al-dhanbu yarīnu raynan," i.e. sin enveloped it; and rayn is like rust covering the heart, and likewise ʿayn. As for the exegetes, they have several views: al-Hasan and Mujahid said: it is sin upon sin, until sins encompass the heart and cover it so that the heart dies. It is narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Beware of the trivial sins, for sin upon sin kindles a huge blaze upon its doer." And from Mujahid: the heart is like the palm; when one commits a sin it contracts, and when he commits another sin it contracts again, then it is sealed upon, and this is rayn. Others said: whenever a person sins, a black spot appears in his heart until the whole heart blackens. This is narrated as a marfu' hadith from Abu Hurayra. I say: there is no doubt that the repetition of acts is a cause for the acquisition of an inner disposition, for whoever wishes to learn writing, the more he practices writing the more perfect his capacity for it becomes, until he reaches the point where he can write without deliberation or thought. This inner disposition, since it was generated from those many acts, each one of those acts has an effect in producing that inner disposition. Having known this, we say: when a person persists in committing some kinds of sin, an inner disposition to commit that sin takes root in his heart, and there is no meaning to sin except what occupies you with other than Allah, and whatever occupies you with other than Allah is darkness; so all sins are darkness and blackness. And each of the past deeds, whose collective result produced that disposition, has an effect in its production. That is what is meant by their saying: whenever a person sins, a black spot appears in his heart until the heart blackens. And since the levels of dispositions differ in intensity and weakness, the levels of this blackness and darkness likewise differ; so some of it is rayn, some is ṭabʿ, and some is iqfāl. The judge said: rayn does not mean that their hearts have changed and an obstruction has occurred in them; rather it means that they became, state after state, bold toward committing sin, their motives to abandon repentance and to refrain grew strong, so they persisted and the matter became difficult for them. That is why He explained that the cause of the rayn is their earning, and it is known that their great acquisition of sins does not prevent them from ceasing and repenting. I say: we have already shown that the occurrence of an act when the motive is equal

to the act, and the motive to abandon it is impossible, because it is impossible for a possible thing to be preponderated without a preponderant cause. So, if it is impossible in the state of being outweighed, it is all the more so. And since al-Qadi conceded that they became, by means of the past deeds, preponderant, it must be that abandoning [sin] in this state is impossible. The full discussion has been presented repeatedly in this book.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay! Indeed, they will be veiled from their Lord that Day﴾, know that they have mentioned several interpretations of (kallā, "nay").

The first: The author of al-Kashshaf said: (kallā) is a deterrent from the gain that has covered over their hearts.

The second: al-Qaffal said: God, exalted is He, related in various surahs about this transgressing sinner that he used to say, "If the Hereafter is true, then God will surely give me wealth and children." Then God, exalted is He, refuted this claim, saying: ﴿Has he looked into the unseen, or has he taken a covenant with the Most Merciful?﴾ [Maryam: 78], and He said: ﴿I do not think the Hour will ever come; and even if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely have a better (reward) with Him﴾ [Fussilat: 50]. Since this has been mentioned repeatedly in the Qur'an, God omitted its mention here and said: ﴿Nay! Indeed, they will be veiled from their Lord that Day﴾, meaning: the matter is not as they claim, that they will have a good reward in the Hereafter; rather, they will be veiled from their Lord that Day.

Third: That this is a repetition, and that this (kallā) is the one mentioned in His saying: ﴿Nay! Rather, what they have earned has rusted over their hearts﴾. As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, they will be veiled from their Lord that Day﴾, the companions (of al-Ash'ari) have argued from it that the believers will see Him, glory be to Him. They said: Were it not so, the specification would have no purpose.

There is another argument, namely that He mentioned this veiling in the context of a threat and warning to the disbelievers, and what is a warning and threat for the disbelievers cannot apply to the believer; therefore this veiling must not apply to the believer. The Mu'tazilah answered this in several ways:

The first: al-Jubba'i said: The intended meaning is that they are veiled from the mercy of their Lord, i.e., prevented, just as it is said in the rules of inheritance: the brothers exclude the mother to a third (yahjubūna al-umm 'ala al-thuluth), and from this it is said of one who prevents entry that he is a ḥājib, because he prevents one from seeing [the ruler].

The second: Abu Muslim said: ﴿Indeed, they will be veiled﴾ means: not brought near. Ḥijāb means rejection, which is the opposite of acceptance, and the meaning is that these deniers of the Resurrection will not be accepted by God. This is what is meant by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor will God speak to them, nor look at them on the Day of Resurrection, nor purify them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 77].

The third: al-Qadi said: Ḥijāb is not an expression for the absence of seeing, for it is said: So-and-so was veiled from the amir, even though he had seen him from a distance. And if ḥijāb is not an expression for the absence of seeing, the argument falls; rather, it must be understood as becoming prevented from finding His mercy, exalted is He.

The fourth: The author of al-Kashshaf said: Their being veiled from Him is an image of contempt for them and humiliation, because access to kings is granted only to those honored in their presence, and only those despised by them are kept away.

The reply: There is no doubt that whoever is prevented from seeing something is said to be veiled from it; and likewise whoever is prevented from entering upon the amir is said to be veiled from him; and likewise it is said that the mother is veiled from the third because of the brothers. When we find these usages, it becomes necessary to take the word as literally applying to a common concept among these instances, to avoid homonymy in the word, and that concept is prevention. In the first case, prevention from seeing occurred; in the second, prevention from reaching nearness to Him; in the third, prevention from entitlement to the third. So the verse's meaning becomes: "Nay! Indeed, they will be prevented from their Lord that Day." Prevention is realized only with respect to what would be established for the servant in relation to God, exalted is He, and that is either knowledge or sight. It cannot be taken to mean knowledge, because that is established for the disbelievers by consensus; therefore it must be taken to mean sight. As for interpreting it as mercy, that is a departure from the apparent meaning without evidence; and likewise what the author of al-Kashshaf said is an abandonment of the apparent meaning without evidence. Then, what confirms the evidence we have mentioned is the statements of the exegetes.

Muqatil said: The meaning of the verse is that after the reckoning and the account, they will not see their Lord, while the believers will see their Lord. Al-Kalbi said: He says they are veiled from looking upon the vision of their Lord, whereas the believer is not veiled from the vision of his Lord. Mālik ibn Anas was asked about this verse and said: Since He veiled His enemies so that they did not see Him, it must be that He manifests Himself to His friends so that they see Him. From al-Shafi'i: Since He veiled a people by wrath, this indicates that another people will see Him by good pleasure.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then indeed they will be burning in Hell﴾, the meaning is: when they become veiled in the place of Resurrection, either from the sight of God according to our view, or from the mercy and honor of God according to the Mu'tazilah, then at that point they are commanded to Hell. Then, when they enter the Fire, they are rebuked for their denial of the Resurrection and the recompense, and it is said to them: ﴿This is what you used to deny﴾ in the world; and now you have witnessed it, so taste it.

Al-Zajjaj said: "rāna ʿalā qulūbihim" means "ghashiya ʿalā qulūbihim" (covered over their hearts); one says "rāna ʿalā qalbihi al-dhanbu yarīnu raynan," i.e. sin enveloped it; and rayn is like rust covering the heart, and likewise ʿayn. As for the exegetes, they have several views: al-Hasan and Mujahid said: it is sin upon sin, until sins encompass the heart and cover it so that the heart dies. It is narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Beware of the trivial sins, for sin upon sin kindles a huge blaze upon its doer." And from Mujahid: the heart is like the palm; when one commits a sin it contracts, and when he commits another sin it contracts again, then it is sealed upon, and this is rayn. Others said: whenever a person sins, a black spot appears in his heart until the whole heart blackens. This is narrated as a marfu' hadith from Abu Hurayra. I say: there is no doubt that the repetition of acts is a cause for the acquisition of an inner disposition, for whoever wishes to learn writing, the more he practices writing the more perfect his capacity for it becomes, until he reaches the point where he can write without deliberation or thought. This inner disposition, since it was generated from those many acts, each one of those acts has an effect in producing that inner disposition. Having known this, we say: when a person persists in committing some kinds of sin, an inner disposition to commit that sin takes root in his heart, and there is no meaning to sin except what occupies you with other than Allah, and whatever occupies you with other than Allah is darkness; so all sins are darkness and blackness. And each of the past deeds, whose collective result produced that disposition, has an effect in its production. That is what is meant by their saying: whenever a person sins, a black spot appears in his heart until the heart blackens. And since the levels of dispositions differ in intensity and weakness, the levels of this blackness and darkness likewise differ; so some of it is rayn, some is ṭabʿ, and some is iqfāl. The judge said: rayn does not mean that their hearts have changed and an obstruction has occurred in them; rather it means that they became, state after state, bold toward committing sin, their motives to abandon repentance and to refrain grew strong, so they persisted and the matter became difficult for them. That is why He explained that the cause of the rayn is their earning, and it is known that their great acquisition of sins does not prevent them from ceasing and repenting. I say: we have already shown that the occurrence of an act when the motive is equal

to the act, and the motive to abandon it is impossible, because it is impossible for a possible thing to be preponderated without a preponderant cause. So, if it is impossible in the state of being outweighed, it is all the more so. And since al-Qadi conceded that they became, by means of the past deeds, preponderant, it must be that abandoning [sin] in this state is impossible. The full discussion has been presented repeatedly in this book.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay! Indeed, they will be veiled from their Lord that Day﴾, know that they have mentioned several interpretations of (kallā, "nay").

The first: The author of al-Kashshaf said: (kallā) is a deterrent from the gain that has covered over their hearts.

The second: al-Qaffal said: God, exalted is He, related in various surahs about this transgressing sinner that he used to say, "If the Hereafter is true, then God will surely give me wealth and children." Then God, exalted is He, refuted this claim, saying: ﴿Has he looked into the unseen, or has he taken a covenant with the Most Merciful?﴾ [Maryam: 78], and He said: ﴿I do not think the Hour will ever come; and even if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely have a better (reward) with Him﴾ [Fussilat: 50]. Since this has been mentioned repeatedly in the Qur'an, God omitted its mention here and said: ﴿Nay! Indeed, they will be veiled from their Lord that Day﴾, meaning: the matter is not as they claim, that they will have a good reward in the Hereafter; rather, they will be veiled from their Lord that Day.

Third: That this is a repetition, and that this (kallā) is the one mentioned in His saying: ﴿Nay! Rather, what they have earned has rusted over their hearts﴾. As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, they will be veiled from their Lord that Day﴾, the companions (of al-Ash'ari) have argued from it that the believers will see Him, glory be to Him. They said: Were it not so, the specification would have no purpose.

There is another argument, namely that He mentioned this veiling in the context of a threat and warning to the disbelievers, and what is a warning and threat for the disbelievers cannot apply to the believer; therefore this veiling must not apply to the believer. The Mu'tazilah answered this in several ways:

The first: al-Jubba'i said: The intended meaning is that they are veiled from the mercy of their Lord, i.e., prevented, just as it is said in the rules of inheritance: the brothers exclude the mother to a third (yahjubūna al-umm 'ala al-thuluth), and from this it is said of one who prevents entry that he is a ḥājib, because he prevents one from seeing [the ruler].

The second: Abu Muslim said: ﴿Indeed, they will be veiled﴾ means: not brought near. Ḥijāb means rejection, which is the opposite of acceptance, and the meaning is that these deniers of the Resurrection will not be accepted by God. This is what is meant by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor will God speak to them, nor look at them on the Day of Resurrection, nor purify them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 77].

The third: al-Qadi said: Ḥijāb is not an expression for the absence of seeing, for it is said: So-and-so was veiled from the amir, even though he had seen him from a distance. And if ḥijāb is not an expression for the absence of seeing, the argument falls; rather, it must be understood as becoming prevented from finding His mercy, exalted is He.

The fourth: The author of al-Kashshaf said: Their being veiled from Him is an image of contempt for them and humiliation, because access to kings is granted only to those honored in their presence, and only those despised by them are kept away.

The reply: There is no doubt that whoever is prevented from seeing something is said to be veiled from it; and likewise whoever is prevented from entering upon the amir is said to be veiled from him; and likewise it is said that the mother is veiled from the third because of the brothers. When we find these usages, it becomes necessary to take the word as literally applying to a common concept among these instances, to avoid homonymy in the word, and that concept is prevention. In the first case, prevention from seeing occurred; in the second, prevention from reaching nearness to Him; in the third, prevention from entitlement to the third. So the verse's meaning becomes: "Nay! Indeed, they will be prevented from their Lord that Day." Prevention is realized only with respect to what would be established for the servant in relation to God, exalted is He, and that is either knowledge or sight. It cannot be taken to mean knowledge, because that is established for the disbelievers by consensus; therefore it must be taken to mean sight. As for interpreting it as mercy, that is a departure from the apparent meaning without evidence; and likewise what the author of al-Kashshaf said is an abandonment of the apparent meaning without evidence. Then, what confirms the evidence we have mentioned is the statements of the exegetes.

Muqatil said: The meaning of the verse is that after the reckoning and the account, they will not see their Lord, while the believers will see their Lord. Al-Kalbi said: He says they are veiled from looking upon the vision of their Lord, whereas the believer is not veiled from the vision of his Lord. Mālik ibn Anas was asked about this verse and said: Since He veiled His enemies so that they did not see Him, it must be that He manifests Himself to His friends so that they see Him. From al-Shafi'i: Since He veiled a people by wrath, this indicates that another people will see Him by good pleasure.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then indeed they will be burning in Hell﴾, the meaning is: when they become veiled in the place of Resurrection, either from the sight of God according to our view, or from the mercy and honor of God according to the Mu'tazilah, then at that point they are commanded to Hell. Then, when they enter the Fire, they are rebuked for their denial of the Resurrection and the recompense, and it is said to them: ﴿This is what you used to deny﴾ in the world; and now you have witnessed it, so taste it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 83, verses 7–17 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Nay! Indeed the record of the wicked is in Sijjin.﴾ ﴿And what will make you know what Sijjin is?﴾ ﴿It is a written record.﴾ ﴿Woe on that day to the deniers,﴾ ﴿who deny the Day of Judgment.﴾ ﴿None deny it except every transgressor, sinful,﴾ ﴿when Our verses are recited to him he says, "Tales of the ancients."﴾ ﴿Nay! Rather, what they used to earn has covered over their hearts.﴾ ﴿Nay! Indeed they, that day, will be veiled from their Lord.﴾ ﴿Then indeed they will be burning in Hellfire.﴾ ﴿Then it will be said, "This is what you used to deny."﴾

Know that when He, glorified is He, explained the magnitude of this sin, He followed it with mention of its consequences and rulings. The first of these is His saying "Nay" (kallā). The exegetes have mentioned several views concerning it.

The first: it is a rebuke and an admonition, meaning the matter is not as they are, in their short-measure and heedlessness regarding the mention of resurrection and reckoning, so let them desist. The complete statement ends here.

The second: Abu Hatim said: "Kallā" is a beginning that connects with what follows, in the sense of "truly, ﴿indeed the record of the wicked is in Sijjin﴾." This is also the view of al-Hasan.

The second type: He, the Exalted, described the record of the wicked with baseness and worthlessness, by way of belittling them. Here there are questions.

The first question: Is Sijjin a proper noun for a specific thing, or a derived noun from a meaning? We say there are two opinions:

The first, which is the view of the majority of exegetes: it is a proper noun for a specific thing. Then they differed about it. Most hold that it is the seventh, lowest earth. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas in the narration of ʿAta', and of Qatada, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd. Al-Bara' narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "Sijjin is the lowest of the seven earths." ʿAta' al-Khurasani said: in it are Iblis and his offspring. Abu Hurayra narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "Sijjin is a pit in Hell." Al-Kalbi and Mujahid said: Sijjin is a rock beneath the seventh earth.

The second opinion: it is derived, named Sijjin as a form of fi‘dl from the prison (sijn), which is confinement and constriction, as one says fisiq from fisq. This is the view of Abu ʿUbayda, al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj. Al-Wahidi said: this is weak, and the evidence that Sijjin is not something the Arabs knew is His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what Sijjin is?﴾, meaning that this is not something you and your people knew. I say: it is not weak, for perhaps He mentioned it only to magnify the matter of Sijjin, as in His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Judgment is?﴾ The author of "al-Kashshaf" said: the correct view is that Sijjin is a fi‘īl form derived from the prison (sijn); then here it is a proper name transferred from an adjective, like Hatim, and it is diptote, because it has only one cause, which is definiteness.

Having known this, we say: We have mentioned that Allah, the Exalted, dealt with His servants in matters according to what they are accustomed to in their dealings among themselves and with their great ones. So Paradise is described with height, purity, spaciousness and the presence of the nearest angels, while Sijjin is described with lowliness, darkness, constriction and the presence of the accursed devils. There is no doubt that height, purity, spaciousness and the presence of the nearest angels are all attributes of perfection and honor, and their opposites are attributes of deficiency and abasement. So when the description of the disbelievers and their record in abasement and worthlessness was intended, it was said that it is in the place of lowliness, darkness, constriction and the presence of devils. And when He described the record of the righteous with honor, it was said that it is ﴿in ʿIlliyyun﴾ and ﴿witnessed by those brought near﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 17].

The second question: Allah has informed about the record of the wicked that it is ﴿in Sijjin﴾, then He explained Sijjin with ﴿a written record﴾. So it is as if it were said: their record is in a written record, so what is its meaning? Al-Qaffal answered: his saying ﴿a written record﴾ is not an explanation of Sijjin; rather the construction is: "Nay! Indeed the record of the wicked is in Sijjin, and indeed the record of the wicked is a written record," so this is a description of the record of the wicked with two attributes: one, that it is in Sijjin; and two, that it is written. And ﴿And what will make you know what Sijjin is?﴾ falls between the two descriptions as a parenthetical interjection. And Allah knows best.

It is better to say: what is strange about one of the two records being within the other? Either the record of the wicked is placed in the book that is the source referred to for detailing the states of the wretched, or what is in the record of the wicked is transferred to that book named Sijjin. There is also a third view: that the intended meaning of "kitāb" is writing, so the sense is: the writing of the wicked is in Sijjin, meaning the writing of their deeds is in Sijjin; then Sijjin is described as ﴿a written record﴾ containing all the deeds of the wicked.

The third question: What is the meaning of His saying ﴿a written record﴾? We say there are several views:

One: "marqūm" means their deeds are written in it.

Second: Qatada said: it was marked for them with evil, meaning it was written for them with the necessity of the Fire.

Third: al-Qaffal said: it may be that what is meant is that He made that record marked, as a merchant marks his garment with a sign of its price; so likewise the record of the wicked is made marked with a mark indicating his wretchedness.

Fourth: "al-marqūm" here means "al-makhtūm" (sealed). Al-Wahidi said: this is correct, because sealing is a sign, so it is permissible to call the marked "sealed."

Fifth: the meaning is a record established upon them like the marking on a garment that does not fade.

As for His saying ﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾, there are two views concerning it:

One: it is connected to His saying ﴿the day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds﴾, meaning: ﴿the day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds﴾, woe to whoever denied the reports of Allah.

Two: His saying "marqūm" means it was marked with a mark indicating wretchedness on the Day of Resurrection; then He said ﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾, on that day, from that record. Then He informed about the description of those who deny the Day of Judgment, saying: ﴿None deny it except every transgressor, sinful, when Our verses are recited to him he says, "Tales of the ancients."﴾ And its meaning is that none denies the Day of Judgment except one who has these three attributes.

The first of them: being a transgressor, and transgression is going beyond the true path.

The second: the sinful, which is an intensive form of committing sin and disobedience. I say: man has two faculties: a theoretical faculty whose perfection lies in knowing the truth for its own sake, and a practical faculty whose perfection lies in knowing the good for the sake of acting upon it. The opposite of the first is to describe Allah with what is not permissible to attribute to Him, for everyone who denies the possibility of resurrection and the Last Day denies either because he did not know that Allah's knowledge encompasses all knowables, universal and particular, or because he did not know that Allah's power extends to all possibilities. So this transgression is the opposite of the practical faculty, namely being occupied with desire and anger, and its possessor is the sinful, because one occupied with desire and anger rarely finds leisure for worship and obedience, and this may well become an obstacle for him to faith in the Last Day.

As for the third attribute of those who deny the Day of Judgment, it is His saying ﴿when Our verses are recited to him he says, "Tales of the ancients."﴾ What is meant are those who deny prophethood. The meaning is: when the Qur'an is recited to him, he says, "Tales of the ancients." And there are two views: one, the falsehoods of the ancients; two, the reports of the ancients, and that it was taken from them, meaning he impugns the Qur'an being from Allah by this route.

Here is another discussion: whether these three attributes refer to a specific person or not. There are two views.
