Indeed, they will be veiled from their Lord that Day﴾, meaning: the matter is not as they claim, that they will have a good reward in the Hereafter; rather, they will be veiled from their Lord that Day.

Third: That this is a repetition, and that this (kallā) is the one mentioned in His saying: ﴿Nay! Rather, what they have earned has rusted over their hearts﴾. As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, they will be veiled from their Lord that Day﴾, the companions (of al-Ash'ari) have argued from it that the believers will see Him, glory be to Him. They said: Were it not so, the specification would have no purpose.

There is another argument, namely that He mentioned this veiling in the context of a threat and warning to the disbelievers, and what is a warning and threat for the disbelievers cannot apply to the believer; therefore this veiling must not apply to the believer. The Mu'tazilah answered this in several ways:

The first: al-Jubba'i said: The intended meaning is that they are veiled from the mercy of their Lord, i.e., prevented, just as it is said in the rules of inheritance: the brothers exclude the mother to a third (yahjubūna al-umm 'ala al-thuluth), and from this it is said of one who prevents entry that he is a ḥājib, because he prevents one from seeing [the ruler].

The second: Abu Muslim said: ﴿Indeed, they will be veiled﴾ means: not brought near. Ḥijāb means rejection, which is the opposite of acceptance, and the meaning is that these deniers of the Resurrection will not be accepted by God. This is what is meant by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor will God speak to them, nor look at them on the Day of Resurrection, nor purify them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 77].

The third: al-Qadi said: Ḥijāb is not an expression for the absence of seeing, for it is said: So-and-so was veiled from the amir, even though he had seen him from a distance. And if ḥijāb is not an expression for the absence of seeing, the argument falls; rather, it must be understood as becoming prevented from finding His mercy, exalted is He.

The fourth: The author of al-Kashshaf said: Their being veiled from Him is an image of contempt for them and humiliation, because access to kings is granted only to those honored in their presence, and only those despised by them are kept away.

The reply: There is no doubt that whoever is prevented from seeing something is said to be veiled from it; and likewise whoever is prevented from entering upon the amir is said to be veiled from him; and likewise it is said that the mother is veiled from the third because of the brothers. When we find these usages, it becomes necessary to take the word as literally applying to a common concept among these instances, to avoid homonymy in the word, and that concept is prevention. In the first case, prevention from seeing occurred; in the second, prevention from reaching nearness to Him; in the third, prevention from entitlement to the third. So the verse's meaning becomes: "Nay! Indeed, they will be prevented from their Lord that Day." Prevention is realized only with respect to what would be established for the servant in relation to God, exalted is He, and that is either knowledge or sight. It cannot be taken to mean knowledge, because that is established for the disbelievers by consensus; therefore it must be taken to mean sight. As for interpreting it as mercy, that is a departure from the apparent meaning without evidence; and likewise what the author of al-Kashshaf said is an abandonment of the apparent meaning without evidence. Then, what confirms the evidence we have mentioned is the statements of the exegetes.

Muqatil said: The meaning of the verse is that after the reckoning and the account, they will not see their Lord, while the believers will see their Lord. Al-Kalbi said: He says they are veiled from looking upon the vision of their Lord, whereas the believer is not veiled from the vision of his Lord. Mālik ibn Anas was asked about this verse and said: Since He veiled His enemies so that they did not see Him, it must be that He manifests Himself to His friends so that they see Him. From al-Shafi'i: Since He veiled a people by wrath, this indicates that another people will see Him by good pleasure.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then indeed they will be burning in Hell﴾, the meaning is: when they become veiled in the place of Resurrection, either from the sight of God according to our view, or from the mercy and honor of God according to the Mu'tazilah, then at that point they are commanded to Hell. Then, when they enter the Fire, they are rebuked for their denial of the Resurrection and the recompense, and it is said to them: ﴿This is what you used to deny﴾ in the world; and now you have witnessed it, so taste it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 83, verses 7–17 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Nay! Indeed the record of the wicked is in Sijjin.﴾ ﴿And what will make you know what Sijjin is?﴾ ﴿It is a written record.﴾ ﴿Woe on that day to the deniers,﴾ ﴿who deny the Day of Judgment.﴾ ﴿None deny it except every transgressor, sinful,﴾ ﴿when Our verses are recited to him he says, "Tales of the ancients."﴾ ﴿Nay! Rather, what they used to earn has covered over their hearts.﴾ ﴿Nay! Indeed they, that day, will be veiled from their Lord.﴾ ﴿Then indeed they will be burning in Hellfire.﴾ ﴿Then it will be said, "This is what you used to deny."﴾

Know that when He, glorified is He, explained the magnitude of this sin, He followed it with mention of its consequences and rulings. The first of these is His saying "Nay" (kallā). The exegetes have mentioned several views concerning it.

The first: it is a rebuke and an admonition, meaning the matter is not as they are, in their short-measure and heedlessness regarding the mention of resurrection and reckoning, so let them desist. The complete statement ends here.

The second: Abu Hatim said: "Kallā" is a beginning that connects with what follows, in the sense of "truly, ﴿indeed the record of the wicked is in Sijjin﴾." This is also the view of al-Hasan.

The second type: He, the Exalted, described the record of the wicked with baseness and worthlessness, by way of belittling them. Here there are questions.

The first question: Is Sijjin a proper noun for a specific thing, or a derived noun from a meaning? We say there are two opinions:

The first, which is the view of the majority of exegetes: it is a proper noun for a specific thing. Then they differed about it. Most hold that it is the seventh, lowest earth. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas in the narration of ʿAta', and of Qatada, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd. Al-Bara' narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "Sijjin is the lowest of the seven earths." ʿAta' al-Khurasani said: in it are Iblis and his offspring. Abu Hurayra narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "Sijjin is a pit in Hell." Al-Kalbi and Mujahid said: Sijjin is a rock beneath the seventh earth.

The second opinion: it is derived, named Sijjin as a form of fi‘dl from the prison (sijn), which is confinement and constriction, as one says fisiq from fisq. This is the view of Abu ʿUbayda, al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj. Al-Wahidi said: this is weak, and the evidence that Sijjin is not something the Arabs knew is His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what Sijjin is?﴾, meaning that this is not something you and your people knew. I say: it is not weak, for perhaps He mentioned it only to magnify the matter of Sijjin, as in His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Judgment is?﴾ The author of "al-Kashshaf" said: the correct view is that Sijjin is a fi‘īl form derived from the prison (sijn); then here it is a proper name transferred from an adjective, like Hatim, and it is diptote, because it has only one cause, which is definiteness.

Having known this, we say: We have mentioned that Allah, the Exalted, dealt with His servants in matters according to what they are accustomed to in their dealings among themselves and with their great ones. So Paradise is described with height, purity, spaciousness and the presence of the nearest angels, while Sijjin is described with lowliness, darkness, constriction and the presence of the accursed devils. There is no doubt that height, purity, spaciousness and the presence of the nearest angels are all attributes of perfection and honor, and their opposites are attributes of deficiency and abasement. So when the description of the disbelievers and their record in abasement and worthlessness was intended, it was said that it is in the place of lowliness, darkness, constriction and the presence of devils. And when He described the record of the righteous with honor, it was said that it is ﴿in ʿIlliyyun﴾ and ﴿witnessed by those brought near﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 17].

The second question: Allah has informed about the record of the wicked that it is ﴿in Sijjin﴾, then He explained Sijjin with ﴿a written record﴾. So it is as if it were said: their record is in a written record, so what is its meaning? Al-Qaffal answered: his saying ﴿a written record﴾ is not an explanation of Sijjin; rather the construction is: "Nay! Indeed the record of the wicked is in Sijjin, and indeed the record of the wicked is a written record," so this is a description of the record of the wicked with two attributes: one, that it is in Sijjin; and two, that it is written. And ﴿And what will make you know what Sijjin is?﴾ falls between the two descriptions as a parenthetical interjection. And Allah knows best.

It is better to say: what is strange about one of the two records being within the other? Either the record of the wicked is placed in the book that is the source referred to for detailing the states of the wretched, or what is in the record of the wicked is transferred to that book named Sijjin. There is also a third view: that the intended meaning of "kitāb" is writing, so the sense is: the writing of the wicked is in Sijjin, meaning the writing of their deeds is in Sijjin; then Sijjin is described as ﴿a written record﴾ containing all the deeds of the wicked.

The third question: What is the meaning of His saying ﴿a written record﴾? We say there are several views:

One: "marqūm" means their deeds are written in it.

Second: Qatada said: it was marked for them with evil, meaning it was written for them with the necessity of the Fire.

Third: al-Qaffal said: it may be that what is meant is that He made that record marked, as a merchant marks his garment with a sign of its price; so likewise the record of the wicked is made marked with a mark indicating his wretchedness.

Fourth: "al-marqūm" here means "al-makhtūm" (sealed). Al-Wahidi said: this is correct, because sealing is a sign, so it is permissible to call the marked "sealed."

Fifth: the meaning is a record established upon them like the marking on a garment that does not fade.

As for His saying ﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾, there are two views concerning it:

One: it is connected to His saying ﴿the day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds﴾, meaning: ﴿the day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds﴾, woe to whoever denied the reports of Allah.

Two: His saying "marqūm" means it was marked with a mark indicating wretchedness on the Day of Resurrection; then He said ﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾, on that day, from that record. Then He informed about the description of those who deny the Day of Judgment, saying: ﴿None deny it except every transgressor, sinful, when Our verses are recited to him he says, "Tales of the ancients."﴾ And its meaning is that none denies the Day of Judgment except one who has these three attributes.

The first of them: being a transgressor, and transgression is going beyond the true path.

The second: the sinful, which is an intensive form of committing sin and disobedience. I say: man has two faculties: a theoretical faculty whose perfection lies in knowing the truth for its own sake, and a practical faculty whose perfection lies in knowing the good for the sake of acting upon it. The opposite of the first is to describe Allah with what is not permissible to attribute to Him, for everyone who denies the possibility of resurrection and the Last Day denies either because he did not know that Allah's knowledge encompasses all knowables, universal and particular, or because he did not know that Allah's power extends to all possibilities. So this transgression is the opposite of the practical faculty, namely being occupied with desire and anger, and its possessor is the sinful, because one occupied with desire and anger rarely finds leisure for worship and obedience, and this may well become an obstacle for him to faith in the Last Day.

As for the third attribute of those who deny the Day of Judgment, it is His saying ﴿when Our verses are recited to him he says, "Tales of the ancients."﴾ What is meant are those who deny prophethood. The meaning is: when the Qur'an is recited to him, he says, "Tales of the ancients." And there are two views: one, the falsehoods of the ancients; two, the reports of the ancients, and that it was taken from them, meaning he impugns the Qur'an being from Allah by this route.

Here is another discussion: whether these three attributes refer to a specific person or not. There are two views.

The first, which is the view of al-Kalbi, is that what is meant is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. Others said it is al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. Those who held that it is al-Walid argued that He said in Surat Nun: ﴿And do not obey every oft-swearing despicable one﴾ up to His saying ﴿transgressor, sinful﴾ up to His saying ﴿when Our verses are recited to him he says, "Tales of the ancients."﴾ [al-Qalam: 10–15], so it was said that this refers to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. On this assumption the meaning is: none of the Quraysh, or of your people, denies the Day of Judgment except every transgressor, sinful; and this is the specific person.

The second view: it is general concerning all who are described with these attributes. As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Nay! Rather, what they used to earn has covered over their hearts﴾, the meaning is: the matter is not as he claims, that these are the tales of the ancients; rather their past deeds became a cause for the rust (rayn) to settle upon their hearts. The lexicographers and the exegetes have several explanations of the word rayn. As for the lexicographers, Abu ʿUbayda said: "rāna ʿalā qulūbihim" means it overcame them, and wine "yarīnu ʿalā" the intellect of the drunkard, and death "yarīnu ʿalā" the dead person so that it takes him away. Al-Layth said: sleep and wine "rāna" in the head when it takes firm hold of it, and it "yarinu" rayvan and ruyūnan. From this is the hadith of ʿUmar concerning Usayfiʿ of Juhayna, when debt overwhelmed him: "He has become overwhelmed by it (qad rīna bihi)." Abu Zayd said: one says "rīna bi-l-rajul yurānu bihi raynan" when he falls into what he cannot get out of. Abu Muʿadh al-Nahwi said: rayn is that the heart becomes blackened by sins, and ṭabʿ is that it is sealed upon the heart, which is stronger than rayn, and iqfāl is stronger than ṭabʿ, being that it is locked upon the heart. Al-Zajjaj said: "rāna ʿalā qulūbihim" means "ghashiya ʿalā qulūbihim" (covered over their hearts); one says "rāna ʿalā qalbihi al-dhanbu yarīnu raynan," i.e. sin enveloped it; and rayn is like rust covering the heart, and likewise ʿayn. As for the exegetes, they have several views: al-Hasan and Mujahid said: it is sin upon sin, until sins encompass the heart and cover it so that the heart dies. It is narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Beware of the trivial sins, for sin upon sin kindles a huge blaze upon its doer." And from Mujahid: the heart is like the palm; when one commits a sin it contracts, and when he commits another sin it contracts again, then it is sealed upon, and this is rayn. Others said: whenever a person sins, a black spot appears in his heart until the whole heart blackens. This is narrated as a marfu' hadith from Abu Hurayra. I say: there is no doubt that the repetition of acts is a cause for the acquisition of an inner disposition, for whoever wishes to learn writing, the more he practices writing the more perfect his capacity for it becomes, until he reaches the point where he can write without deliberation or thought. This inner disposition, since it was generated from those many acts, each one of those acts has an effect in producing that inner disposition. Having known this, we say: when a person persists in committing some kinds of sin, an inner disposition to commit that sin takes root in his heart, and there is no meaning to sin except what occupies you with other than Allah, and whatever occupies you with other than Allah is darkness; so all sins are darkness and blackness. And each of the past deeds, whose collective result produced that disposition, has an effect in its production. That is what is meant by their saying: whenever a person sins, a black spot appears in his heart until the heart blackens. And since the levels of dispositions differ in intensity and weakness, the levels of this blackness and darkness likewise differ; so some of it is rayn, some is ṭabʿ, and some is iqfāl. The judge said: rayn does not mean that their hearts have changed and an obstruction has occurred in them; rather it means that they became, state after state, bold toward committing sin, their motives to abandon repentance and to refrain grew strong, so they persisted and the matter became difficult for them. That is why He explained that the cause of the rayn is their earning, and it is known that their great acquisition of sins does not prevent them from ceasing and repenting. I say: we have already shown that the occurrence of an act when the motive is equal

to the act, and the motive to abandon it is impossible, because it is impossible for a possible thing to be preponderated without a preponderant cause. So, if it is impossible in the state of being outweighed, it is all the more so. And since al-Qadi conceded that they became, by means of the past deeds, preponderant, it must be that abandoning [sin] in this state is impossible. The full discussion has been presented repeatedly in this book.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay! Indeed, they will be veiled from their Lord that Day﴾, know that they have mentioned several interpretations of (kallā, "nay").

The first: The author of al-Kashshaf said: (kallā) is a deterrent from the gain that has covered over their hearts.

The second: al-Qaffal said: God, exalted is He, related in various surahs about this transgressing sinner that he used to say, "If the Hereafter is true, then God will surely give me wealth and children." Then God, exalted is He, refuted this claim, saying: ﴿Has he looked into the unseen, or has he taken a covenant with the Most Merciful?﴾ [Maryam: 78], and He said: ﴿I do not think the Hour will ever come; and even if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely have a better (reward) with Him﴾ [Fussilat: 50]. Since this has been mentioned repeatedly in the Qur'an, God omitted its mention here and said: ﴿Nay! Indeed, they will be veiled from their Lord that Day﴾, meaning: the matter is not as they claim, that they will have a good reward in the Hereafter; rather, they will be veiled from their Lord that Day.

Third: That this is a repetition, and that this (kallā) is the one mentioned in His saying: ﴿Nay! Rather, what they have earned has rusted over their hearts﴾. As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, they will be veiled from their Lord that Day﴾, the companions (of al-Ash'ari) have argued from it that the believers will see Him, glory be to Him. They said: Were it not so, the specification would have no purpose.

There is another argument, namely that He mentioned this veiling in the context of a threat and warning to the disbelievers, and what is a warning and threat for the disbelievers cannot apply to the believer; therefore this veiling must not apply to the believer. The Mu'tazilah answered this in several ways:

The first: al-Jubba'i said: The intended meaning is that they are veiled from the mercy of their Lord, i.e., prevented, just as it is said in the rules of inheritance: the brothers exclude the mother to a third (yahjubūna al-umm 'ala al-thuluth), and from this it is said of one who prevents entry that he is a ḥājib, because he prevents one from seeing [the ruler].

The second: Abu Muslim said: ﴿Indeed, they will be veiled﴾ means: not brought near. Ḥijāb means rejection, which is the opposite of acceptance, and the meaning is that these deniers of the Resurrection will not be accepted by God. This is what is meant by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor will God speak to them, nor look at them on the Day of Resurrection, nor purify them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 77].

The third: al-Qadi said: Ḥijāb is not an expression for the absence of seeing, for it is said: So-and-so was veiled from the amir, even though he had seen him from a distance. And if ḥijāb is not an expression for the absence of seeing, the argument falls; rather, it must be understood as becoming prevented from finding His mercy, exalted is He.

The fourth: The author of al-Kashshaf said: Their being veiled from Him is an image of contempt for them and humiliation, because access to kings is granted only to those honored in their presence, and only those despised by them are kept away.

The reply: There is no doubt that whoever is prevented from seeing something is said to be veiled from it; and likewise whoever is prevented from entering upon the amir is said to be veiled from him; and likewise it is said that the mother is veiled from the third because of the brothers. When we find these usages, it becomes necessary to take the word as literally applying to a common concept among these instances, to avoid homonymy in the word, and that concept is prevention. In the first case, prevention from seeing occurred; in the second, prevention from reaching nearness to Him; in the third, prevention from entitlement to the third. So the verse's meaning becomes: "Nay! Indeed, they will be prevented from their Lord that Day." Prevention is realized only with respect to what would be established for the servant in relation to God, exalted is He, and that is either knowledge or sight. It cannot be taken to mean knowledge, because that is established for the disbelievers by consensus; therefore it must be taken to mean sight. As for interpreting it as mercy, that is a departure from the apparent meaning without evidence; and likewise what the author of al-Kashshaf said is an abandonment of the apparent meaning without evidence. Then, what confirms the evidence we have mentioned is the statements of the exegetes.

Muqatil said: The meaning of the verse is that after the reckoning and the account, they will not see their Lord, while the believers will see their Lord. Al-Kalbi said: He says they are veiled from looking upon the vision of their Lord, whereas the believer is not veiled from the vision of his Lord. Mālik ibn Anas was asked about this verse and said: Since He veiled His enemies so that they did not see Him, it must be that He manifests Himself to His friends so that they see Him. From al-Shafi'i: Since He veiled a people by wrath, this indicates that another people will see Him by good pleasure.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then indeed they will be burning in Hell﴾, the meaning is: when they become veiled in the place of Resurrection, either from the sight of God according to our view, or from the mercy and honor of God according to the Mu'tazilah, then at that point they are commanded to Hell. Then, when they enter the Fire, they are rebuked for their denial of the Resurrection and the recompense, and it is said to them: ﴿This is what you used to deny﴾ in the world; and now you have witnessed it, so taste it.

**Verses 18–21:**

﴿Nay, indeed the record of the righteous is in ʿIlliyyūn.﴾ ﴿And what will make you know what ʿIlliyyūn is?﴾ ﴿It is a written record,﴾ ﴿witnessed by those brought near [to God].﴾

Know that when God, exalted is He, mentioned the state of the wicked defrauders (al-fujjār al-muṭaffifīn), He followed it with the state of the righteous (al-abrār), who do not defraud. He said: ﴿Nay﴾, meaning the matter is not as those wicked people imagined, in denying the resurrection and in claiming that the Book of God is "tales of the ancients."

Know that the lexicographers (ahl al-lughah) have several opinions on the word ﴿ʿIlliyyūn﴾, and the exegetes (ahl al-tafsīr, the scholars of Qur'anic interpretation) also have several opinions. As for the lexicographers, Abū al-Fatḥ al-Mawṣilī said: "ʿIlliyyūn" is the plural of ʿilliyy, which is fiʿlīl from ʿuluww (highness). Al-Zajjāj said: The grammatical inflection (iʿrāb) of this noun is like that of a plural, because it is in the form of a plural, just as you say: hādhihi qinnisrūna, and I saw qinnisrīna.

As for the exegetes, it is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that it is the seventh heaven, and in another narration that it is the fourth heaven. Qatādah and Muqātil said: it is the right pillar of the Throne, above the seventh heaven. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it is the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntahā). Al-Farrāʾ said: it means elevation after elevation with no end to it. Al-Zajjāj said: it is the highest of places. Others said: it is lofty ranks, protected by majesty, which God has exalted and whose status He has raised high. Others said: it is with the book of the deeds of the angels.

The apparent meaning of the Qur'an supports this last opinion, because God said to His Messenger: ﴿And what will make you know what ʿIlliyyūn is?﴾, as an indication that it is known to him and that he will come to know it. Then He said: ﴿It is a written record﴾, ﴿witnessed by those brought near [to God]﴾. Thus He made clear that their record is in this written book, which is witnessed by the angels brought near. It is as if God, just as He entrusted them with the Preserved Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ), similarly entrusts them with preserving the books of the righteous within that book, which is the Mother of the Book (umm al-kitāb), as an honouring of it. It is also not impossible that when the recording angels ascend with the books of the righteous, they hand them over to these brought-near angels, who preserve them just as they preserve their own records; or they transcribe what is in those pages into that book which they were entrusted to preserve, and their knowledge becomes testimony for these righteous people. Therefore they are reckoned with an easy reckoning, because these brought-near angels testify on their behalf to what they have preserved of their deeds. And if this book is in the heavens, then the saying of one who interprets it as being in the lofty heaven is correct, so the opinions converge on this. And if that is so, what we have mentioned is the better view.

Know that the reliable position in the interpretation of this verse is what we have explained: that elevation, spaciousness, light and purity are signs of happiness, while lowness, narrowness, and darkness are signs of misery. Since the purpose of placing the book of the wicked in the lowest of the low and in the most confined places is to humiliate the wicked and belittle their status, the purpose of placing the book of the righteous in the highest ʿIlliyyūn, and of the angels bearing witness to it, is to honour them and magnify their status.

There is another interpretation of the verse: that by "the book" is meant "the writing," so the meaning is that the writing of the deeds of the righteous is in ʿIlliyyūn. Then He described ʿIlliyyūn as "a written record," in which are all the deeds of the righteous. This is the view of Abū Muslim.

As for His saying ﴿It is a written record﴾, there are two interpretations. The first: that the "written record" refers to the book of their deeds.

The second: that it is a book placed in ʿIlliyyūn, in which is written what God has prepared for them of honour and reward. They differed about that book. Muqātil said: those things are written for them on the leg of the Throne. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that it is written on a tablet of emerald (zabarjad) suspended beneath the Throne. Others said: it is a book written with that which brings them joy, the opposite of the inscribing of the book of the wicked with that which distresses them. This meaning is supported by His saying ﴿witnessed by those brought near [to God]﴾, meaning the angels who are in ʿIlliyyūn, who witness and attend that written record. As for the one who says it is the book of deeds, he says: the brought-near angels witness that book when it is raised up to ʿIlliyyūn, as an honour for the believer.

**Verses 18–21:**

﴿Nay, indeed the record of the righteous is in ʿIlliyyūn.﴾ ﴿And what will make you know what ʿIlliyyūn is?﴾ ﴿It is a written record,﴾ ﴿witnessed by those brought near [to God].﴾

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 83, verse 22–28:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss﴾ ﴿on couches, observing﴾ ﴿You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾ ﴿They will be given to drink of a pure sealed wine﴾ ﴿whose seal is musk; and for that let the competitors compete﴾ ﴿and its mixture is from Tasnim﴾ ﴿a spring from which those brought near will drink﴾.

Know that when He, glorified and exalted, had magnified their record in the previous verse, He magnified their station with this verse, saying: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss﴾. Then He described the manner of that bliss by three matters, the first of which is His saying: ﴿on couches, observing﴾. Al-Qaffal said: "The arā'ik (couches) are beds within canopies, and according to what they claimed, a arīkah is not called by that name unless it is like this." And from al-Hasan: "We did not know what the arīkah was until we met a man from the people of Yemen who informed us that the arīkah among them is that."

As for His saying (yanzurūn, "observing"), there are three aspects to it.

The first: they observe the varieties of their blessings in Paradise, from the wide-eyed houris and the youths, and the kinds of food, drink, garments, mounts and other things. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The believer looks and encompasses all that Allah has given him, and the least of them sees before him the like of the expanse of this world."

The second: Muqatil said: they observe their enemy as they are being punished in the Fire.

The third: whenever they desire something, they look at it, and that thing is present for them at once. Know that these three aspects are of one genus, namely the thing looked at, so it is obligatory to apply the word to all of them. There occurs to my mind a fourth interpretation, which is nobler than all of them: that they look upon their Lord. This interpretation is reinforced by what He said after this verse: ﴿You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾, and the looking that is connected with radiance is the vision of Allah, Exalted, as He said: ﴿Faces that day will be radiant, looking at their Lord﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22–23].

Page 90
Among what reinforces this interpretation is that it is necessary to begin with mention of the greatest of pleasures, and that is nothing but the vision of Allah, Exalted? Second: His saying, Exalted: ﴿You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾, and in it are two issues:

The first issue: the meaning is that when you see them you know that they are people of blessing, because of the signs visible in their faces that indicate this. Then concerning those signs there are two views:

One of them: it is the laughter and joyfulness seen in their faces, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿Faces that day will be bright, laughing, rejoicing﴾ [Abasa: 38].

The second: 'Ata' said: Allah, Exalted, increases in their faces light, beauty and whiteness beyond what any describer can describe. The explanation of nadrah has already passed under His saying: ﴿radiant﴾.

The second issue: it is read (tu'raf, "is recognized") in the passive voice, and (jannātu al-naʿīm, "gardens of bliss") in the nominative.

Third: His saying: ﴿They will be given to drink of a pure﴾, and in it are two issues:

The first issue: explaining what the rahīq (pure wine) is. Al-Layth said: "al-Rahiq" is wine. And he recited a verse of Hassan:

Barada flows with the pure, unmixed rahiq.

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Zajjaj said: "al-Rahiq" is the wine that has no adulteration in it and nothing that spoils it, and perhaps it is the wine that Allah described with His saying: ﴿neither is there in it any intoxication﴾ [al-Saffat: 47].
The second issue: Allah mentioned for this rahiq attributes:

The first attribute: His saying: ﴿sealed﴾, and in it are several views. The first: Al-Qaffal said: it is possible that these are given to drink from a sealed drink that has been sealed upon as an honor to it by way of protection, according to the custom of sealing what is honored and guarded. And there is another wine from which rivers flow, as He said: ﴿and rivers of wine, delicious to the drinkers﴾ [Muhammad: 15], except that this sealed one is nobler in what flows.

The second: Abu 'Ubaydah, al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj said: the sealed one is that which has a khitām, that is, an outcome.

The third: It is narrated from 'Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) regarding makhtum that it means mixed. Al-Wahidi said: this is not an explanation, because sealing does not have mixing as its explanation, but since it has an outcome which is the scent of musk, he explained it as mixed, because if it were not mixed with musk, the scent of musk would not have come into it.

The fourth: Mujahid said: makhtum means sealed with clay. Al-Wahidi said: it seems his meaning by sealing with clay is that no hand touches it until the righteous break its seal. The closest of all these views is the first one mentioned by al-Qaffal.

The second attribute of this rahiq is His saying: ﴿whose seal is musk﴾, and in it are views:

The first: Al-Qaffal said: its meaning is that what seals the mouth of that rahiq's flask is musk, like the clay with which the mouths of flasks are sealed, so that musk was moist, and the seal would be impressed in it. This view corresponds to the first view we related from al-Qaffal in explaining His saying: ﴿sealed﴾.

The second: The intended meaning of His saying: ﴿whose seal is musk﴾, that is, its outcome is musk, meaning its end is sealed for it with the scent of musk. This view corresponds to the view we related from Abu 'Ubaydah in explaining His saying: ﴿sealed﴾. It is as if He, exalted, said: "from a rahiq which has an outcome," then explained that outcome, saying: "that outcome is musk," meaning whoever drinks it, the end of his drinking is upon the scent of musk. This is the saying of 'Alqamah, al-Dahhak, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Muqatil and Qatadah, who said: when the drinker lifts his mouth from the end of his drink, he finds its scent like the scent of musk, and the meaning is the delightfulness of the aftertaste, the fragrance of the smell and its pleasantness, along with the goodness of the taste. The khitām is the last of everything, and from it one says: "I completed (khatamtu) the Qur'an," and "deeds are by their endings." This is confirmed by the reading of 'Ali, peace be upon him, and the choice of al-Kisa'i, for he reads: "khātamuhu misk" (its seal is musk), meaning its last part, as one says "khātam al-nabiyyīn" (the seal of the prophets). Al-Farra' said: the two are close in meaning, except that khātam is a noun and khitām is a verbal noun, like their saying: "he is noble of character (ṭibā')" and "ṭābi'."

The third: its meaning is that it is mixed with musk, and they mentioned that in it is a perfuming of its taste. It was also said: rather, of its scent. I say: perhaps what is meant is that wine mixed with these hot spices helps digestion and strengthens desire, so perhaps what is meant by it is an indication of the strength of their desire and the health of their bodies. This view was related by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from al-Aswad from 'Aishah: a woman says, "I have taken the khatm of clay," meaning, I have taken the mixtures of clay. Abu al-Darda' said: it is a white drink like silver, with which they seal the end of their drinking. If a man of the people of this world were to put his hand into it and then take it out, no living soul would remain without finding the sweetness of its scent.

The second attribute: His saying, Exalted: ﴿And for that let the competitors compete﴾. Al-Wahidi said: it is said: "I begrudged him the thing (nafistu 'alayhi al-shay') and became covetous of it (nafāsah)" when you withhold it and do not love that it should go to him, and tanāfus is a reciprocal form of it, as though each of the two persons wants to monopolize it. The meaning: for that let those who desire desire it by hastening to obey Allah.

Know that Allah's exaggeration in encouraging toward it indicates the loftiness of its status, and there is in it an indication that competition ought to be for such great and lasting bliss, not for bliss that is turbid and swiftly perishing.

The fourth attribute: His saying, Exalted: ﴿and its mixture is from Tasnim﴾, and in it are issues:

The first issue: Tasnim is a proper name for a specific spring in Paradise, named "Tasnim," which is the verbal noun of sannamahu, meaning "he raised it." Either because it is the most elevated drink in Paradise; or because it comes to them from above, according to what is related that it flows in the air raised high and pours into their vessels; or because, owing to the abundance and speed of its filling, it rises above everything it passes, and that is its tasnim; or because when it flows there appears in it a rising and falling, and so it is tasnim as well. This is because the root of this word is for height and elevation, from which comes sanam al-ba'ir (the hump of the camel), and tasannamtu al-ha'it (I climbed the wall). As for the statement of the exegetes: Maymun ibn Mihran related that Ibn 'Abbas was asked about Tasnim, and he said: "This is of what Allah says: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for the eyes﴾ [al-Sajdah: 17]." Close to this is what al-Hasan said: it is a matter that Allah concealed for the people of Paradise. Al-Wahidi said: according to this, it has no known derivation and it is a proper noun. And from 'Ikrimah: "min tasnim" means "from honor."

The second issue: He, exalted, mentioned that Tasnim is a spring from which those brought near drink. Ibn 'Abbas said: the most noble drink of the people of Paradise is Tasnim, because those brought near drink it pure, and it is mixed for the companions of the right.

Know that when Allah, Exalted, divided the responsible persons in Surah al-Waqi'ah into three categories: those brought near, the companions of the right, and the companions of the left, then when He mentioned the honor of those mentioned in this surah, that their drink is mixed from a spring from which those brought near drink, we knew that those mentioned in this place are the companions of the right. I say: this indicates that the rivers differ in excellence; Tasnim is the most excellent of the rivers of Paradise, and those brought near are the most excellent of the people of Paradise. Tasnim in the spiritual Paradise is the knowledge of Allah and the delight of looking at the noble Face of Allah, while the rahiq is the joy of contemplating the world of existents. So those brought near drink only from Tasnim, that is, they occupy themselves only with contemplating His noble Face, while the companions of the right have their drink mixed, so at times their gaze is upon Him and at other times upon His creatures.

The third issue: ("ʿaynan," a spring) is in the accusative as a praise. al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. And His saying: ﴿a spring from which those brought near will drink﴾ is like His saying: ﴿a spring from which the servants of Allah will drink﴾ [al-Insan: 6], and it has passed.

This view corresponds to the first view we related from al-Qaffal in explaining His saying: ﴿sealed﴾.

The second: The intended meaning of His saying: ﴿whose seal is musk﴾, that is, its outcome is musk, meaning its end is sealed for it with the scent of musk. This view corresponds to the view we related from Abu 'Ubaydah in explaining His saying: ﴿sealed﴾. It is as if He, exalted, said: "from a rahiq which has an outcome," then explained that outcome, saying: "that outcome is musk," meaning whoever drinks it, the end of his drinking is upon the scent of musk. This is the saying of 'Alqamah, al-Dahhak, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Muqatil and Qatadah, who said: when the drinker lifts his mouth from the end of his drink, he finds its scent like the scent of musk, and the meaning is the delightfulness of the aftertaste, the fragrance of the smell and its pleasantness, along with the goodness of the taste. The khitām is the last of everything, and from it one says: "I completed (khatamtu) the Qur'an," and "deeds are by their endings." This is confirmed by the reading of 'Ali, peace be upon him, and the choice of al-Kisa'i, for he reads: "khātamuhu misk" (its seal is musk), meaning its last part, as one says "khātam al-nabiyyīn" (the seal of the prophets). Al-Farra' said: the two are close in meaning, except that khātam is a noun and khitām is a verbal noun, like their saying: "he is noble of character (ṭibā')" and "ṭābi'."

The third: its meaning is that it is mixed with musk, and they mentioned that in it is a perfuming of its taste. It was also said: rather, of its scent. I say: perhaps what is meant is that wine mixed with these hot spices helps digestion and strengthens desire, so perhaps what is meant by it is an indication of the strength of their desire and the health of their bodies. This view was related by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from al-Aswad from 'Aishah: a woman says, "I have taken the khatm of clay," meaning, I have taken the mixtures of clay. Abu al-Darda' said: it is a white drink like silver, with which they seal the end of their drinking. If a man of the people of this world were to put his hand into it and then take it out, no living soul would remain without finding the sweetness of its scent.

The second attribute: His saying, Exalted: ﴿And for that let the competitors compete﴾. Al-Wahidi said: it is said: "I begrudged him the thing (nafistu 'alayhi al-shay') and became covetous of it (nafāsah)" when you withhold it and do not love that it should go to him, and tanāfus is a reciprocal form of it, as though each of the two persons wants to monopolize it. The meaning: for that let those who desire desire it by hastening to obey Allah.

Know that Allah's exaggeration in encouraging toward it indicates the loftiness of its status, and there is in it an indication that competition ought to be for such great and lasting bliss, not for bliss that is turbid and swiftly perishing.

The fourth attribute: His saying, Exalted: ﴿and its mixture is from Tasnim﴾, and in it are issues:

The first issue: Tasnim is a proper name for a specific spring in Paradise, named "Tasnim," which is the verbal noun of sannamahu, meaning "he raised it." Either because it is the most elevated drink in Paradise; or because it comes to them from above, according to what is related that it flows in the air raised high and pours into their vessels; or because, owing to the abundance and speed of its filling, it rises above everything it passes, and that is its tasnim; or because when it flows there appears in it a rising and falling, and so it is tasnim as well. This is because the root of this word is for height and elevation, from which comes sanam al-ba'ir (the hump of the camel), and tasannamtu al-ha'it (I climbed the wall). As for the statement of the exegetes: Maymun ibn Mihran related that Ibn 'Abbas was asked about Tasnim, and he said: "This is of what Allah says: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for the eyes﴾ [al-Sajdah: 17]." Close to this is what al-Hasan said: it is a matter that Allah concealed for the people of Paradise. Al-Wahidi said: according to this, it has no known derivation and it is a proper noun. And from 'Ikrimah: "min tasnim" means "from honor."

The second issue: He, exalted, mentioned that Tasnim is a spring from which those brought near drink. Ibn 'Abbas said: the most noble drink of the people of Paradise is Tasnim, because those brought near drink it pure, and it is mixed for the companions of the right.

Know that when Allah, Exalted, divided the responsible persons in Surah al-Waqi'ah into three categories: those brought near, the companions of the right, and the companions of the left, then when He mentioned the honor of those mentioned in this surah, that their drink is mixed from a spring from which those brought near drink, we knew that those mentioned in this place are the companions of the right. I say: this indicates that the rivers differ in excellence; Tasnim is the most excellent of the rivers of Paradise, and those brought near are the most excellent of the people of Paradise. Tasnim in the spiritual Paradise is the knowledge of Allah and the delight of looking at the noble Face of Allah, while the rahiq is the joy of contemplating the world of existents. So those brought near drink only from Tasnim, that is, they occupy themselves only with contemplating His noble Face, while the companions of the right have their drink mixed, so at times their gaze is upon Him and at other times upon His creatures.

The third issue: ("ʿaynan," a spring) is in the accusative as a praise. al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. And His saying: ﴿a spring from which those brought near will drink﴾ is like His saying: ﴿a spring from which the servants of Allah will drink﴾ [al-Insan: 6], and it has passed.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 83, verse 29–36:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed﴾ ﴿And when they passed by them, they winked at one another﴾ ﴿And when they returned to their people, they returned jesting﴾ ﴿And when they saw them, they said, "Indeed, these are strayed"﴾ ﴿But they had not been sent as guardians over them﴾ ﴿So today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers﴾ ﴿On couches, looking on﴾ ﴿Have the disbelievers been repaid for what they used to do?﴾ Know that when He, glorified is He, described the honour of the righteous in the Hereafter, He then mentioned the ugliness of the treatment the disbelievers gave them in this world, in their mockery and laughter. Then He explained that this would be reversed upon the disbelievers in the Hereafter. The purpose of this is to console the believers and strengthen their hearts. There are several issues in this:

The first issue: they mentioned two reports concerning the occasion of revelation:

The first: that what is meant by His saying ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes﴾ is the chief polytheists, such as Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah and al-As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi, who used to laugh at Ammar, Suhayb, Bilal and others among the poor Muslims, and mock them.

The second: 'Ali (peace be upon him) came with a group of Muslims, and the hypocrites ridiculed them, laughed, and winked at one another. Then they returned to their companions and said: "Today we saw the bald one," and they laughed at him. So this verse was revealed before 'Ali reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The second issue: He, exalted is He, related four of their ugly dealings.

The first of them is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed﴾, meaning they mocked them and their religion.

The second is His saying: ﴿And when they passed by them, they winked at one another﴾, meaning they make gestures to one another, from ghamz, which is signalling with the eyelid and the eyebrow. Ghamz also means finding fault, and "ghamaza him" means he found fault with him; and "ma fi fulan ghamizah" means there is nothing in so-and-so to be faulted for. The meaning is that they gestured at them with their eyes in mockery and found fault with them, saying: "Look at these people who tire themselves, deprive themselves of its pleasures, and risk themselves in pursuit of a reward they are not certain of."

The third is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they returned to their people, they returned jesting﴾, being pleased with what they were in of polytheism, sin, and worldly luxury; or they took delight in speaking ill of the Muslims. Asim, in the narration of Hafs from him, read "fakihin" without an alif in this place alone, and in the rest of the Qur'an "fakihin" with an alif. The rest read "fakihin" with an alif. It is said that both are dialectal forms. It is also said: "fakihin" means luxuriating and preoccupied with what they were in of disbelief and worldly luxury, and "fakihin" means pleased with themselves.

The fourth is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they saw them, they said, "Indeed, these are strayed"﴾, meaning they are in error in abandoning present luxury for the sake of a reward of which it is not known whether it exists or not. This is the last of what He, exalted is He, related of the disbelievers.

Page 93

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿But they had not been sent as guardians over them﴾, meaning that Allah, exalted is He, did not send these disbelievers as watchers over the believers, observing their conditions and scrutinizing what they do, whether right or wrong, so that they find fault with them for what they believe to be error. Rather, they were only commanded to reform themselves.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers﴾, there are two issues in it:

The first issue: the meaning is that on this day, which is the day when deeds are weighed and reckoning takes place, the believer laughs at the disbeliever. There are several views on the cause of this laughter:

One of them: the disbelievers used to laugh at the believers in this world because of their harm and misery, and in the Hereafter the believers laugh at the disbelievers because of the various kinds of punishment and affliction they are in. Also, because they knew that they had been in this world upon nothing, and that they had sold what remains for what perishes, while they see themselves as having won everlasting bliss and attained eternal comfort through little hardship. They have entered Paradise and are seated on couches, looking at them: how they are punished in the Fire, how they cry out there, calling for destruction and perdition, and how some of them curse one another.

The second: Abu Salih said: It is said to the people of the Fire while they are in it: "Come out." Its gates are opened for them, and when they see that it has been opened, they approach it wanting to leave. The believers look at them from the couches. When they reach its gates, they are shut in their faces. That is the cause of the laughter.

The second issue: His saying: ﴿On couches, looking on﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "they laugh", meaning they laugh at them while looking at them and at what they are in of humiliation and abasement after their might and arrogance.

* * *

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿Have the disbelievers been repaid for what they used to do?﴾ Thuwwiba here means utheeba, that is, Allah the Rewarder rewarded them. Aws said:

"I will repay you, or a rewarder will repay you on my behalf, and it is enough for you that you be praised and commended."

Al-Mubarrad said: it is fu'ila from al-thawab, which is that which returns to its doer as recompense for what he did of good or evil. Thawab is also used for requital with evil. Abu Ubaydah recited:

"Oh, convey to Abu Hasan a message: why do you not come to the thawab?"

The better view is that this is to be taken as sarcasm, like His saying: ﴿Taste, indeed you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [al-Dukhan: 49]. The meaning is as if He, exalted is He, is saying to the believers: "Have We repaid the disbelievers for their deeds, of which part was their laughing at you and mocking your way, just as We have repaid you for your good deeds?" This statement adds to their joy, because it implies an increase in their honour and the belittling of their enemies. Its purpose is the states of the Resurrection. And Allah knows best.
